Budgeted Multi-Source Counterfactual Annotation
for Off-Policy Evaluation

Biao Xiang ††thanks: Corresponding author. Email: bqx5053@psu.edu    Ali Eshragh ††thanks: Equal supervision. Affiliation: Johns Hopkins Carey Business School, Washington, DC Affiliation: International Computer Science Institute, Berkeley, CA    Yuexing Li    Kai Wang    [0.1em] Pennsylvania State University    State College    PA Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA
Abstract

Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the value of a target policy from logged data, but limited behavior-policy coverage can force high-variance reweighting or reward-model extrapolation. Counterfactual annotations can add evidence about unobserved actions, yet practical sources, including domain experts and large language models (LLMs), may be costly, biased, or noisy. We study budgeted acquisition of such annotations for contextual-bandit OPE. Given source-specific costs and error profiles, we formulate an integer allocation problem over context-action pairs and annotation sources to minimize the component of estimator variance that depends on the annotation plan. We characterize when annotations are valuable through a first-annotation threshold and local annotation-value regimes. For the coupled multi-source problem, we develop a majorization-minimization algorithm with dynamic-programming subroutines that monotonically improves the objective. Experiments in synthetic clinical and LLM-annotated education bandits show that our allocation method reduces fixed-profile mean squared error (MSE) by 20.58%20.58\% and 10.77%10.77\%, respectively, relative to no annotation.

1 Introduction

Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the value of a target policy from data collected by a different behavior policy. It is especially important when online evaluation is expensive, disruptive, or risky, as in healthcare and education. In contextual bandits, logged data reveal rewards only for actions selected by the behavior policy. When the target policy assigns probability to actions that are poorly covered in the logged data, evaluation can depend on high-variance reweighting, reward-model extrapolation, or both.

Counterfactual annotations offer a practical way to add evidence about unobserved actions without deploying the target policy. For example, a clinician may assess what would likely have happened under an alternative treatment, or an automated tutor may estimate a student’s response under a different instructional activity. Recent work has shown how such annotations can be incorporated into OPE estimators [1, 2]. However, a key practical question remains: when annotations are costly and imperfect, which ones should be collected?

This question matters because annotation sources vary in cost and reliability. Domain experts may be accurate but expensive, while large language models (LLMs) may scale cheaply yet make systematic errors on particular context-action pairs. In the counterfactual-annotated estimator we study, such errors do not introduce bias into the policy-value estimate but affect variance through the reward model. Annotation value therefore depends jointly on source quality, cost, factual coverage, and how strongly the target policy weights the annotated action.

We formulate counterfactual-annotation acquisition as a budget-constrained allocation problem: given estimates of each source’s cost, bias, and variability, choose which context-action pairs to annotate and which sources to query so as to minimize the part of the estimation error that depends on the annotation plan. The problem is discrete because annotations are acquired one at a time, and coupled because annotations for different actions in the same context jointly shape the reward model used for evaluation. These challenges require both a statistical understanding of when annotations are valuable and an optimization method for allocating them under budget. To address them, we make three contributions:

  1. (I)

    Annotation-value regimes. We derive a first-annotation threshold and a four-regime characterization of when annotations help immediately, help only up to a finite amount, help only after acquiring a sufficiently large batch, or do not help locally.

  2. (II)

    Budgeted allocation algorithm. We show that the allocation problem is coupled, nonconvex, and not generally submodular, and develop a majorization-minimization (MM) algorithm with dynamic-programming subroutines that monotonically improves the original objective.

  3. (III)

    Empirical validation. Across synthetic and LLM-annotated bandit environments, we compare against greedy allocation and certified solver benchmarks, quantify profile-estimation sensitivity, and validate the final OPE estimator using finite pilots and independent evaluation samples.

2 Related Work

Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the value of a target policy from data generated by a behavior policy. Core estimators include importance sampling and per-decision variants [19], direct-method estimators that learn reward, value, or transition models [25, 26], and doubly robust (DR) estimators that combine model estimates with importance-weighted corrections [11, 12, 7]. Variance reduction and reliability have been further studied through data-efficient DR estimators [24, 13], representation-based OPE [27], empirical benchmarking [28], and confidence or estimator-selection methods [23, 22, 14, 17]. Our work builds on this OPE foundation, but addresses the acquisition stage: which counterfactual annotations to collect before applying the estimator.

A related stream augments logged data with counterfactual or auxiliary information. Structural-causal methods construct counterfactual trajectories [10, 18]; semi-offline OPE reweights human counterfactual annotations to preserve the logged context distribution [1]; and CANDOR incorporates imperfect annotations into DR contextual-bandit estimators, particularly through the reward model [2]. Auxiliary-data methods such as trajectory augmentation, PERRY, and APRIL use generated trajectories or LLM-derived predictions for inference and policy evaluation [9, 15, 16, 4]. These works study how to use auxiliary information once available; we study how to allocate a finite annotation budget across heterogeneous sources.

Our problem is also related to budgeted data acquisition: active learning and optimal design choose measurements under resource constraints [21, 20], while multiple-logger OPE combines logged data from different behavior policies [8]. Our setting differs because the acquired data are counterfactual rewards used in a DR reward model, rather than supervised labels or additional logged actions. Thus, annotation value is not standalone informativeness; it is defined by how the annotation changes the resulting OPE estimator’s variance under the target and behavior policies.

5 Annotation Value: Thresholds, Regimes, and Multi-Source Benefits

Before solving problem (3), we examine when counterfactual annotations are statistically valuable. We first study a single context-action pair and source to derive the first-annotation threshold (§5.1) and four regimes of annotation value (§5.2). These results motivate source selection and bias cancellation (§5.3), followed by an analysis of cross-action coupling in the full allocation problem (§5.4).

5.1 Local Single-Source Objective and First-Annotation Threshold

To gain actionable insight, we first focus on a single context-action pair (s,a)(s,a) with nf​(s,a)>0n_{f}(s,a)>0 and α1​(s,a)>0\alpha_{1}(s,a)>0, and a single annotation source gg. The case nf​(s,a)=0n_{f}(s,a)=0 is discussed in Appendix B.8. For ease of notation, we suppress the dependence on (s,a)(s,a) throughout and write nf:=nf​(s,a)n_{f}:=n_{f}(s,a), ε:=εg​(s,a)\varepsilon:=\varepsilon_{g}(s,a), Δ:=Δg​(s,a)\Delta:=\Delta_{g}(s,a), σ2:=σr2​(s,a)\sigma^{2}:=\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a), σg2:=σ2+Δ\sigma_{g}^{2}:=\sigma^{2}+\Delta, η:=η⁡(s,a)\eta:=\eta(s,a), and αi:=αi​(s,a)\alpha_{i}:=\alpha_{i}(s,a) for i=1,3i=1,3. For nn annotations, the (s,a)(s,a) terms of J1+J3J_{1}+J_{3} give the local objective

ϕ⁡(n):=α1​n2​ε2+α3​(nf​σ2+n​σg2)(nf+n)2.\phi(n):=\frac{\alpha_{1}n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}\bigl(n_{f}\sigma^{2}+n\sigma_{g}^{2}\bigr)}{(n_{f}+n)^{2}}. (5)

We omit J2J_{2} here because it couples actions within the same context, and revisit its effect in §5.4. By isolating this local scenario, we derive a threshold condition under which adding the first annotation does not increase the local objective (5).

Theorem 3 (First Annotation Threshold).

The first annotation, corresponding to the transition n=0n=0 to n=1n=1, does not increase the local objective (5) if and only if

ε2​(s,a)≤η⁡(s,a)​((nf​(s,a)+1)​σ2​(s,a)nf​(s,a)−Δ⁡(s,a)),\varepsilon^{2}(s,a)\leq\eta(s,a)\!\left(\frac{(n_{f}(s,a)+1)\sigma^{2}(s,a)}{n_{f}(s,a)}-\Delta(s,a)\right), (6)

where η⁡(s,a)=1−πb​(a∣s)\eta(s,a)=1-\pi_{b}(a\mid s). In particular, if Δ⁡(s,a)≥(nf​(s,a)+1)​σ2/nf​(s,a)\Delta(s,a)\geq(n_{f}(s,a)+1)\sigma^{2}/n_{f}(s,a), then δ​ϕ​(0)>0\delta\phi(0)>0 for every (s,a) with ε⁡(s,a)≠0\varepsilon(s,a)\neq 0.

The threshold explains why the same source can be useful at one pair but not another: its bias is judged against the variance reduction available at that pair. Greater factual coverage lowers the factor (nf+1)/nf(n_{f}+1)/n_{f}, while greater excess variance reduces the remaining variance benefit; both make the first annotation harder to justify. Appendix B.3 gives the proof.

5.2 Four Regimes of Annotation Value

The first-annotation threshold compares only ϕ⁡(1)\phi(1) with ϕ⁡(0)\phi(0). To understand how annotation value evolves as more annotations are added, we now characterize the behavior of the local objective ϕ⁡(n)\phi(n) over all annotation counts. Although nn is integer-valued in the allocation problem, treating it as continuous reveals the marginal structure of ϕ⁡(n)\phi(n). Differentiating (5) gives ϕ′​(n)=(𝔞​n+𝔟)/(nf+n)3\phi^{\prime}(n)=(\mathfrak{a}\,n+\mathfrak{b})/(n_{f}+n)^{3}, where 𝔞:=2​α1​ε2​nf−α3​σg2\mathfrak{a}:=2\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}-\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2} and 𝔟:=α3​nf​(Δ−σ2)\mathfrak{b}:=\alpha_{3}n_{f}(\Delta-\sigma^{2}). Thus, the sign of ϕ′​(n)\phi^{\prime}(n) is determined by the affine term 𝔞​n+𝔟\mathfrak{a}n+\mathfrak{b}, yielding four possible regimes.

Theorem 4 (Four Regimes of Annotation Value).

In all cases, ϕ⁡(n)→α1​ε2\phi(n)\to\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2} as n→∞n\to\infty. When 𝔞=𝔟=0\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{b}=0, ϕ\phi is constant; otherwise, it falls into four regimes:

  1. (I)

    If 𝔞≥0\mathfrak{a}\geq 0 and 𝔟≥0\mathfrak{b}\geq 0, then ϕ\phi is increasing, so annotations are locally harmful.

  2. (II)

    If 𝔞>0\mathfrak{a}>0 and 𝔟<0\mathfrak{b}<0, then ϕ\phi decreases and then increases, with unique continuous minimizer n∗=η​nf​(σ2−Δ)/(2​ε2​nf−η​σg2)n^{*}=\eta n_{f}(\sigma^{2}-\Delta)/(2\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}-\eta\sigma_{g}^{2}).

  3. (III)

    If 𝔞≤0\mathfrak{a}\leq 0 and 𝔟≤0\mathfrak{b}\leq 0, then ϕ\phi is decreasing, so each annotation locally reduces the objective.

  4. (IV)

    If 𝔞<0\mathfrak{a}<0 and 𝔟>0\mathfrak{b}>0, then ϕ\phi first increases and then decreases, with unique continuous maximizer n¯=η​nf​(Δ−σ2)/(η​σg2−2​ε2​nf)\bar{n}=\eta n_{f}(\Delta-\sigma^{2})/(\eta\sigma_{g}^{2}-2\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}). In this regime, a strict improvement over no annotation is possible if and only if ε2<η​σ2/nf\varepsilon^{2}<\eta\sigma^{2}/n_{f}.

Regime (II) favors a finite count, so spending the entire available budget on one pair can be counterproductive. In Regime (IV), a sufficiently large batch improves on no annotation only if the limiting bias contribution satisfies α1​ε2<ϕ⁡(0)\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}<\phi(0) (IVa); otherwise, n=0n=0 remains best (IVb). Table 1 translates these distinctions into local allocation decisions, subject to the available budget and capacities; Appendix B.4 gives the proof.

5.3 Source Selection and Bias Cancellation

The local regimes reveal how access to multiple sources can improve allocation. Because every single-source plan remains feasible under the same budget and capacities, the multi-source optimum is no worse than the best single-source optimum. To identify where source selection can help, we apply the first-annotation threshold (6) to source kk:

εgk​(s,a)2≤η⁡(s,a)​((nf​(s,a)+1)​σr2​(s,a)nf​(s,a)−Δgk​(s,a)).\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(s,a)^{2}\;\leq\;\eta(s,a)\!\left(\frac{(n_{f}(s,a)+1)\,\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a)}{n_{f}(s,a)}-\Delta_{g_{k}}(s,a)\right). (7)

Because factual coverage and source quality vary across pairs, condition (7) can hold for different sources at different pairs.

Sources can also complement one another within a pair. At a fixed total annotation count, mixing two sources with opposite-signed biases can reduce the magnitude of the reward-model bias B⁡(s,a,𝐧)=∑knk​(s,a)​εgk​(s,a)/N⁡(s,a)B(s,a;\mathbf{n})=\sum_{k}n_{k}(s,a)\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(s,a)/N(s,a) below that obtained from either source alone. The allocation must balance this reduction against source variances and costs. When one source performs well across pairs and mixing offers little bias cancellation, gains over the best single source can be modest.

5.4 From Local Thresholds to the Full Allocation Problem

The benefits of source selection and mixing must be evaluated through the full objective, which includes cross-action coupling through J2J_{2}. For α3>0\alpha_{3}>0 and zero aggregate reward-model bias in context ss, including J2J_{2} changes the first-annotation threshold to ε2≤(nf+1)​σ2/nf−Δ\varepsilon^{2}\leq(n_{f}+1)\sigma^{2}/n_{f}-\Delta, removing the factor η\eta from Theorem 3 and permitting larger admissible bias when the right-hand side is positive. More generally, the marginal effect of J2J_{2} depends on the effective biases of all actions in the same context, while source mixing can reduce B⁡(s,a,𝐧)B(s,a;\mathbf{n}) via bias cancellation but reshapes ℬs​(𝐧)\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}). Together with the shared budget, this coupling motivates the joint allocation method in §6.

6 Budget-Constrained Multi-Source Allocation

We now solve the multi-source allocation problem (3). Proposition 1 formalizes why the local rules from §5 cannot be applied independently: the problem has cross-action coupling, nonconvexity, and integer constraints.

Proposition 1 (Structure of the allocation objective).

The objective J⁡(𝐧)J(\mathbf{n}) in problem (3) is nonnegative and bounded over all feasible allocations. Moreover, there exist valid instances for which:

  1. (I)

    JJ is non-separable across actions within the same context.

  2. (II)

    The continuous relaxation of JJ is neither convex nor concave.

  3. (III)

    JJ is neither submodular nor supermodular over annotation allocations.

An annotation’s full value depends on the other allocations in its context, so independent pairwise decisions need not produce a good joint allocation. We use majorization-minimization (MM) [29] to replace the cross-action coupling by a locally tight upper surrogate while retaining the exact per-pair bias-variance structure. Feasible surrogate-improving updates then guarantee monotone descent. Appendices C and D.2 give the structural proofs and descent analysis, respectively.

6.1 Majorization-Minimization Surrogate

We optimize the objective JJ using an iterative MM scheme. Starting from a feasible allocation 𝐧(0)\mathbf{n}^{(0)} (zero or a greedy allocation), each MM iteration constructs an upper bound around 𝐧(t)\mathbf{n}^{(t)} and seeks a feasible update that improves this surrogate. The term −J2-J_{2} is the only part of JJ that couples actions within the same context through ℬs​(𝐧)2\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})^{2}. We majorize this coupling term, turning it into an affine function of ℬs​(𝐧)\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}) while leaving J1J_{1} and J3J_{3} unchanged. The following proposition shows that this replacement yields an upper bound that is exact at the current allocation.

Proposition 2 (Tight majorization of JJ).

Fix a feasible allocation 𝐧(t)\mathbf{n}^{(t)} at iteration tt and let ℬs(t):=ℬs​(𝐧(t))\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(t)}:=\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}). Define J~full​(𝐧,𝐧(t))=J1​(𝐧)+J3​(𝐧)+∑s∈𝒮d0​(s)​[(ℬs(t))2−2​ℬs(t)​ℬs​(𝐧)].\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})=J_{1}(\mathbf{n})+J_{3}(\mathbf{n})+\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\bigl[(\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(t)})^{2}-2\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(t)}\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})\bigr]. Then J~full\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}} is a tight upper bound on JJ: J~full​(𝐧,𝐧(t))−J⁡(𝐧)=∑s∈𝒮d0​(s)​(ℬs​(𝐧)−ℬs(t))2≥0.\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})-J(\mathbf{n})=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\bigl(\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})-\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(t)}\bigr)^{2}\geq 0. In particular, J~full​(𝐧(t),𝐧(t))=J⁡(𝐧(t))\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})=J(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}).

Tightness at the current allocation ensures that a feasible update improving the surrogate cannot increase JJ. For computation, we drop the allocation-independent constant ∑sd0​(s)​(ℬs(t))2\sum_{s}d_{0}(s)(\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(t)})^{2}, obtaining the equivalent surrogate

J~​(𝐧,𝐧(t))=J1​(𝐧)+J3​(𝐧)−2​∑s∈𝒮d0​(s)​ℬs(t)​ℬs​(𝐧).\displaystyle\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})=J_{1}(\mathbf{n})+J_{3}(\mathbf{n})-2\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(t)}\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}). (8)

Substituting ℬs​(𝐧)=∑aπe​(a|s)​B​(s,a,𝐧)\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})=\sum_{a}\pi_{e}(a|s)B(s,a;\mathbf{n}) into (8) shows that J~\tilde{J} is additively separable in (s,a)(s,a). Each iteration therefore searches for an improving allocation using these separable costs under the original constraints, preserving descent in JJ. Appendix D.2 gives the majorization proof.

6.2 Solving the Surrogate Allocation Problem

We now describe the computational step at a fixed MM iteration tt. We write J~​(𝐧,𝐧(t))=∑s,aJ~s,a(t)​(𝐧s,a)\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})=\sum_{s,a}\tilde{J}_{s,a}^{(t)}(\mathbf{n}_{s,a}), where J~s,a(t)\tilde{J}_{s,a}^{(t)} denotes the summand of J~\tilde{J} specific to the context-action pair (s,a)(s,a), and 𝐧s,a:=(n1​(s,a),…,nK​(s,a))\mathbf{n}_{s,a}:=(n_{1}(s,a),\ldots,n_{K}(s,a)) is the source-count vector. The remaining challenge is to handle the shared budget and capacity constraints.

Let C⁡(𝐧):=∑s,a,kck​nk​(s,a)C(\mathbf{n}):=\sum_{s,a,k}c_{k}n_{k}(s,a) denote the total annotation cost. For a fixed multiplier λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, we minimize the penalized surrogate J~​(𝐧,𝐧(t))+λ​C​(𝐧)\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})+\lambda C(\mathbf{n}), while retaining the per-context and context-action capacity constraints. Thus, the penalized problem decomposes by context. For each context-action pair (s,a)(s,a) and each feasible annotation count m∈{0,…,Ns−nf​(s,a)}m\in\{0,\ldots,N_{s}-n_{f}(s,a)\}, define Hs,a(t,λ)(m):=min𝐳∈ℤ+K: 1⊤​𝐳=m{J~s,a(t)(𝐳)+λ∑k=1Kckzk}.H_{s,a}^{(t,\lambda)}(m):=\min_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{K}:\,\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{z}=m}\bigl\{\tilde{J}_{s,a}^{(t)}(\mathbf{z})+\lambda\sum_{k=1}^{K}c_{k}z_{k}\bigr\}. Here, 𝐳=(z1,…,zK)\mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{K}) specifies how the mm annotations for (s,a)(s,a) are split across sources, and the local surrogate is evaluated with N⁡(s,a)=nf​(s,a)+mN(s,a)=n_{f}(s,a)+m. Thus, Hs,a(t,λ)​(m)H_{s,a}^{(t,\lambda)}(m) is the best penalized surrogate value among all source mixtures that assign exactly mm annotations to (s,a)(s,a). Exact enumeration over all source-count vectors 𝐳\mathbf{z} yields a certified solution for Hs,a(t,λ)​(m)H_{s,a}^{(t,\lambda)}(m), but the cost grows combinatorially with KK. We instead obtain approximate values Hs,a♯​(m,λ)H^{\sharp}_{s,a}(m,\lambda) by pairwise-exchange local search, which reallocates one annotation between sources at a time to reduce the penalized surrogate while keeping mm fixed. Proposition 9 in Appendix D.3 bounds the resulting approximation error.

Given Hs,a(t,λ)​(m)H_{s,a}^{(t,\lambda)}(m), it remains to choose how many annotations each context-action pair receives within context ss. Let ms,a:=∑k=1Knk​(s,a)m_{s,a}:=\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a) denote the total number of annotations assigned to (s,a)(s,a), aggregated over sources. For each context, the remaining problem is

min⁡∑a∈𝒜{ms,a}a∈𝒜⁡Hs,a(t,λ)​(ms,a)s.t.∑a∈𝒜ms,a≤Ns,ms,a∈{0,…,Ns−nf​(s,a)},∀a∈𝒜.\displaystyle\min_{\{m_{s,a}\}_{a\in\mathcal{A}}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}H_{s,a}^{(t,\lambda)}(m_{s,a})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}m_{s,a}\leq N_{s},\quad m_{s,a}\in\{0,\ldots,N_{s}-n_{f}(s,a)\},~\forall a\in\mathcal{A}.

We solve the aggregation by dynamic programming (DP), using H♯H^{\sharp} in place of HH and allowing unused context capacity. DP is exact for these tables; the source mixtures remain approximate.

We search over λ\lambda by bisection. Each trial value of λ\lambda returns a candidate allocation from the penalized problem above, computed by local source search followed by DP across actions within each context. Among the candidates satisfying C⁡(𝐧)≤κC(\mathbf{n})\leq\kappa, together with the current allocation 𝐧(t)\mathbf{n}^{(t)}, we select the one with the smallest surrogate value J~​(⋅,𝐧(t))\tilde{J}(\cdot;\mathbf{n}^{(t)}). Because 𝐧(t)\mathbf{n}^{(t)} is included as a fallback, the selected update 𝐧(t+1)\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)} satisfies J~​(𝐧(t+1),𝐧(t))≤J~​(𝐧(t),𝐧(t))\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})\leq\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)}) and hence J⁡(𝐧(t+1))≤J⁡(𝐧(t))J(\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)})\leq J(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}). We assess allocation quality by benchmarking against exact solvers. The evaluation of the empirical optimality gaps is detailed in §7. We next bound the computational cost of an MM update.

Proposition 3 (Runtime per MM update).

Let TBisT_{\mathrm{Bis}} denote the total number of multiplier trials and let Tswap≥1T_{\mathrm{swap}}\geq 1 bound the number of annotation reassignments per local search. One MM update costs 𝒪⁡(TBis​|𝒮|​|𝒜|​(K2​Nmax​Tswap+Nmax2))\mathcal{O}\!\bigl(T_{\mathrm{Bis}}\,|\mathcal{S}|\,|\mathcal{A}|\,(K^{2}N_{\max}\,T_{\mathrm{swap}}+N_{\max}^{2})\bigr), where Nmax:=maxs⁡Ns≥1N_{\max}:=\max_{s}N_{s}\geq 1.

The terms K2​Nmax​TswapK^{2}N_{\max}T_{\mathrm{swap}} and Nmax2N_{\max}^{2} correspond to local source search and DP aggregation, respectively. With the other parameters fixed, the runtime bound grows linearly with the number of context-action pairs. Appendices D.7 and D.1 give the proof and pseudocode.

7 Numerical Experiments

We evaluate 1) how source quality affects annotation value, 2) how MM compares with greedy and solver benchmarks, and 3) how profile-estimation error affects final OPE performance. For comparisons with fixed source profiles, we report scaled total MSE of the estimator (1), 𝒱⁡(𝐧)=N​MSE​(𝐧)=N​C0+J⁡(𝐧)\mathcal{V}(\mathbf{n})=N\,\mathrm{MSE}(\mathbf{n})=NC_{0}+J(\mathbf{n}). Full experimental details are deferred to Appendix E.

7.1 Annotation Value and Synthetic Validation

We construct a synthetic clinical bandit with 100100 contexts, 55 actions, M=1,000M=1{,}000 fitting records, and budget κ=10,000\kappa=10{,}000. Detailed environment settings are in Appendix E.1.

To illustrate the four regimes in Theorem 4, we construct four sources combining low or high bias with low or high excess variance (Table 2). For each source kk and pair (s,a)(s,a), we independently draw bias and excess variance from normal distributions parameterized by εk\varepsilon_{k} and Δk\Delta_{k}, respectively.

We activate one source at a time and randomly allocate increasing numbers of its annotations to examine how scaled MSE changes. We average over 100100 independently sampled environments.

Figure 1 matches the predicted regimes: Source 1 decreases monotonically (Regime III), Source 2 first increases and then decreases (Regime IV), Source 3 decreases and then increases (Regime II), and Source 4 increases monotonically (Regime I). The decomposition shows how variance reduction (J3J_{3}) competes with bias accumulation (J1J_{1}) and correction (J2J_{2}).

We next examine how the set of available annotation sources affects allocation quality. We evaluate all 2K−1=152^{K}-1=15 nonempty source subsets 𝒦sub⊆{1,2,3,4}\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{sub}}\subseteq\{1,2,3,4\} from Table 2. For multi-source subsets, we run the proposed MM algorithm in §6 restricted to the active sources. For single-source subsets, we use a uniformly random allocation (assigning annotations uniformly across eligible logged samples and counterfactual actions until the budget or per-sample capacity is reached) as a non-optimized baseline; the corresponding optimized single-source results are reported in Appendix E.1.2. All runs use the same environment, factual data, and budget κ=10,000\kappa=10{,}000.

Figure 2 shows that the four-source setting achieves the lowest scaled MSE among the evaluated subsets, illustrating the potential benefit of source selection and mixing discussed in §5.3. With fixed source profiles, the four-source MM allocation reduces scaled MSE from 𝒱⁡(𝟎)=84.23\mathcal{V}(\mathbf{0})=84.23 to 66.9066.90, corresponding to a 20.58%20.58\% MSE reduction relative to no annotation. Full convergence traces are provided in Appendix E.1.3.

7.2 Baselines and Solver Benchmarks

To compare allocation methods with realistic annotation sources, we also construct a semi-synthetic education bandit from 6.16.1 million ASSISTments student–problem interactions [5]. Contexts are |𝒮|=100|\mathcal{S}|=100 K-means clusters of student answer history and affect features, including past correct rate, hint usage, and detector confidences for frustration, confusion, concentration, and boredom. Actions are the |𝒜|=10|\mathcal{A}|=10 problem_type×\timesoriginal combinations.

Following the feature-prediction approach of APRIL [4], each LLM predicts the student’s first-response time tt, which is converted to reward through R⁡(s,a,t)=Rmax⋅PIRT​(s,a)⋅TimeEff⁡(t,t~a)R(s,a,t)=R_{\max}\cdot P_{\mathrm{IRT}}(s,a)\cdot\mathrm{TimeEff}(t,\tilde{t}_{a}). Here, Rmax=30R_{\max}=30 and PIRT​(s,a)=σ⁡(θs−ba)P_{\mathrm{IRT}}(s,a)=\sigma(\theta_{s}-b_{a}) is a one-parameter logistic item response theory (IRT) model [3], with context-level ability θs\theta_{s} and action difficulty bab_{a}. The factor TimeEff⁡(t,t~a)=max⁡{0.3, 1−0.4​|log10⁡(t/t~a)|}\mathrm{TimeEff}(t,\tilde{t}_{a})=\max\{0.3,\,1-0.4|\log_{10}(t/\tilde{t}_{a})|\} discounts responses that are much faster or slower than action aa’s empirical median response time t~a\tilde{t}_{a}.

We use Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4o-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5 as annotation sources, collecting 2020 predictions per source and (s,a)(s,a) to estimate εgk​(s,a)\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(s,a) and Δgk​(s,a)\Delta_{g_{k}}(s,a). Appendix E.2 details the data processing, reward construction, LLM prompts, and MM algorithm results.

For the baselines, Greedy (max-gain) repeatedly selects the feasible annotation with largest positive marginal gain, while Greedy (cost-aware) uses gain per unit cost. We compare these methods with zero-initialized MM and MM initialized from the better greedy allocation on the ASSISTments, original synthetic, and I/IV-focused synthetic environments. The I/IV-focused environment tests allocation with locally harmful or initially harmful sources, for which single-annotation gains can be uninformative. Within each environment, all methods use the same budget, capacities, source costs, and source profiles.

Table 3 shows that MM or greedy-initialized MM achieves the lowest MSE in each environment, with reductions of 10.77%10.77\%, 20.68%20.68\%, and 16.11%16.11\% relative to no annotation. On the I/IV-focused instance, MM improves on both greedy baselines, illustrating the value of jointly allocating annotations beyond single-step gains.

To assess how close these allocations are to a global optimum, we construct 3030 small instances with 55 contexts, 33 actions, and 2525 logged samples. For each instance, we enumerate the feasible context-level choices and use Gurobi to solve the resulting multiple-choice knapsack mixed-integer linear program to certified global optimality. Table 4 shows that greedy-initialized MM has the lowest mean optimality gap. On the full Synthetic and ASSISTments instances, it reaches within 0.2807%0.2807\% and 0.0050%0.0050\% of the Gurobi lower bounds, respectively (Appendix E.3).

7.3 Robustness to Finite-Pilot Profile Estimation

The preceding comparisons use fixed source profiles; we now test whether the gains persist when profiles are estimated from finite pilots. Across 3030 pilot replications, factual moments are estimated from 2020 pilot rewards per pair and annotation moments from 2020 pilot draws per source–pair. The pilot, reward-model fitting data, acquired annotations, and OPE evaluation data are mutually independent. After selecting an allocation, we evaluate DM+-IS using 5050 independent final estimates per pilot replication. Greedy-initialized MM performs best, reducing empirical OPE MSE by 19.13%19.13\% on Synthetic and 8.47%8.47\% on ASSISTments relative to no annotation.

As a complementary sensitivity check, we perform 3030 within-pair bootstraps of the 2020 observed LLM predictions and rerun MM after re-estimating every source profile. On ASSISTments, the resulting mean reference-profile scaled-MSE reduction is 10.765%10.765\%, compared with 10.774%10.774\% using the original profiles, with a standard deviation of only 0.00380.0038 percentage points. The bootstrap indicates stable allocation quality under resampling of the observed LLM outputs, complementing the gains in final OPE MSE measured with independent evaluation data. Full protocols and baseline results are reported in Appendices E.4 and E.5.

8 Conclusion

We formulated budgeted counterfactual annotation for contextual-bandit off-policy evaluation as an integer allocation problem minimizing the MSE of the DM+​-​IS\mathrm{DM}^{+}\text{-}\mathrm{IS} estimator. The objective separates effective annotation bias, cross-action bias correction, and reward/annotation variance, explaining why annotation sources are not interchangeable. For a single context-action pair and source, we derived a first-annotation threshold and four annotation-value regimes. For multiple sources, we established cross-action coupling, nonconvexity, and lack of submodularity, and developed a majorization-minimization algorithm with dynamic-programming subroutines that monotonically improves the objective. These results guide the purchase and allocation of counterfactual annotations under a limited budget to improve policy evaluation.

Limitations and future work. Our framework is limited to contextual bandits and uses known or estimated source profiles (εgk,Δgk)(\varepsilon_{g_{k}},\Delta_{g_{k}}). The ASSISTments experiment uses real LLM annotations in a semi-synthetic environment. Future work includes sequential Markov decision processes, online estimation of source profiles, and human annotations in fully real-world experiments.
