Appendix A Derivations for the Objective Function

This appendix provides the full, step-by-step derivations for the explicit forms of the variance decomposition described in the main text. Throughout the appendices, we interpret πe​(a|s)/πb​(a|s)\pi_{e}(a|s)/\pi_{b}(a|s) and πe​(a|s)2/πb​(a|s)\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}/\pi_{b}(a|s) as zero whenever πe​(a|s)=0\pi_{e}(a|s)=0, consistent with the coefficient convention preceding (2).

Recall that variance of the DM+​-IS\text{DM}^{+}\text{-IS} estimator is decomposed as:

N​Var⁡(v^DM+​-IS​(πe))\displaystyle N\operatorname{Var}\left(\hat{v}^{\text{DM}^{+}\text{-IS}}(\pi_{e})\right) =Vars∼d0⁡(v⁡(πe|s))\displaystyle=\operatorname{Var}_{s\sim d_{0}}(v(\pi_{e}|s))
+𝔼s∼d0[𝔼a∼πb(⋅|s)[ρ(s,a)2σr2(s,a)]]\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{0}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{b}(\cdot|s)}\left[\rho(s,a)^{2}\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a)\right]\right]
+𝔼s∼d0[𝔼a∼πb(⋅|s)[ρ(s,a)2ε^r^+(s,a)2]−ε^r^+πe(s)2]\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{0}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{b}(\cdot|s)}\left[\rho(s,a)^{2}\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}(s,a)^{2}\right]-\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}^{\pi_{e}}(s)^{2}\right]
+𝔼s∼d0[𝔼a∼πb(⋅|s)[(ρ(s,a)2−πe​(a|s)2πb​(a|s))×Var𝒟(r^+(s,a))]]\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{0}}\Bigg[\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{b}(\cdot|s)}\Bigg[\left(\rho(s,a)^{2}-\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}\right)\times\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal{D}}\left(\hat{r}^{+}(s,a)\right)\Bigg]\Bigg]

The total variance is decomposed as follows:

N​Var⁡(v^DM+​-IS​(πe))=T1+T2+T3+T4N\operatorname{Var}\left(\hat{v}^{\text{DM}^{+}\text{-IS}}(\pi_{e})\right)=T_{1}+T_{2}+T_{3}+T_{4}

where T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} can be seen as constant with respect to 𝐧\mathbf{n}. We focus on deriving the explicit forms of T3T_{3} and T4T_{4}.

In addition, as proved in  [2], v^DM+​-IS​(πe)\hat{v}^{\text{DM}^{+}\text{-IS}}(\pi_{e}) remain unbiased even the annotations are biased. Thus,

MSE⁡(𝐧)=0+Var⁡(v^DM+​-IS​(πe))=C0+J⁡(𝐧)N,\operatorname{MSE}(\mathbf{n})=0+\operatorname{Var}\left(\hat{v}^{\text{DM}^{+}\text{-IS}}(\pi_{e})\right)=C_{0}+\frac{J(\mathbf{n})}{N},

where C0=Vars∼d0(v(πe|s))+𝔼s∼d0[𝔼a∼πb(⋅|s)[ρ(s,a)2σr2(s,a)]]NC_{0}=\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{s\sim d_{0}}(v(\pi_{e}|s))+\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{0}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{b}(\cdot|s)}\left[\rho(s,a)^{2}\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a)\right]\right]}{N}.

A.1 Term 3

The third term is given by:

T3=𝔼s∼d0[𝔼a∼πb(⋅|s)[ρ(s,a)2ε^r^+(s,a)2]−ε^r^+πe(s)2]T_{3}=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{0}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{b}(\cdot|s)}\left[\rho(s,a)^{2}\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}(s,a)^{2}\right]-\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}^{\pi_{e}}(s)^{2}\right] (9)

First, we derive the bias ε^r^+​(s,a)\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}(s,a) for a pair with N⁡(s,a)>0N(s,a)>0. We begin by calculating the expectation 𝔼𝒟​[r^+​(s,a)]\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\hat{r}^{+}(s,a)]:

𝔼𝒟​[r^+​(s,a)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\hat{r}^{+}(s,a)] =1N⁡(s,a)​(∑i=1nf​(s,a)𝔼⁡[ri]+∑k=1K∑j=1nk​(s,a)𝔼⁡[gk,j])\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N(s,a)}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n_{f}(s,a)}\mathbb{E}[r_{i}]+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{k}(s,a)}\mathbb{E}[g_{k,j}]\right)
=1N⁡(s,a)​(nf​(s,a)​μr​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​(μr​(s,a)+εgk​(s,a)))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N(s,a)}\left(n_{f}(s,a)\mu_{r}(s,a)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)(\mu_{r}(s,a)+\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(s,a))\right)
=1N⁡(s,a)​(nf​(s,a)​μr​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​μr​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​εgk​(s,a))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N(s,a)}\left(n_{f}(s,a)\mu_{r}(s,a)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\mu_{r}(s,a)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(s,a)\right)
=1N⁡(s,a)​((nf​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a))​μr​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​εgk​(s,a))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N(s,a)}\left(\left(n_{f}(s,a)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\right)\mu_{r}(s,a)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(s,a)\right)
=1N⁡(s,a)​(N⁡(s,a)​μr​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​εgk​(s,a))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N(s,a)}\left(N(s,a)\mu_{r}(s,a)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(s,a)\right)
=μr​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​εgk​(s,a)N⁡(s,a).\displaystyle=\mu_{r}(s,a)+\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(s,a)}{N(s,a)}.

The bias term ε^r^+​(s,a)\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}(s,a) is defined as:

ε^r^+​(s,a)\displaystyle\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}(s,a) :=𝔼𝒟​[r^+​(s,a)]−μr​(s,a)\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\hat{r}^{+}(s,a)]-\mu_{r}(s,a)
=(μr​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​εgk​(s,a)N⁡(s,a))−μr​(s,a)\displaystyle=\left(\mu_{r}(s,a)+\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(s,a)}{N(s,a)}\right)-\mu_{r}(s,a)
=∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​εgk​(s,a)N⁡(s,a)\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(s,a)}{N(s,a)} (10)

If N⁡(s,a)=0N(s,a)=0, the fixed default instead gives ε^r^+​(s,a)=r0​(s,a)−μr​(s,a)\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}(s,a)=r_{0}(s,a)-\mu_{r}(s,a). Thus ε^r^+​(s,a)=B⁡(s,a,𝐧)\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}(s,a)=B(s,a;\mathbf{n}) in both cases, using the definition preceding (2). Next, we derive ε^r^+πe​(s)\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}^{\pi_{e}}(s) by expanding the expectation over the target policy πe\pi_{e}:

ε^r^+πe​(s)\displaystyle\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}^{\pi_{e}}(s) :=𝔼a∼πe(⋅|s)[ε^r^+(s,a)]\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{e}(\cdot|s)}[\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}(s,a)]
=∑a∈𝒜πe​(a|s)​ε^r^+​(s,a)\displaystyle=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{e}(a|s)\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}(s,a)
=∑a∈𝒜πe​(a|s)​B​(s,a,𝐧)\displaystyle=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{e}(a|s)B(s,a;\mathbf{n}) (11)

Substituting these bias expressions into (9) gives

T3\displaystyle T_{3} =∑s∈𝒮d0(s)(𝔼a∼πb(⋅|s)[ρ(s,a)2ε^r^+(s,a)2]−(ε^r^+πe(s))2)\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\left(\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{b}(\cdot|s)}\left[\rho(s,a)^{2}\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}(s,a)^{2}\right]-\left(\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}^{\pi_{e}}(s)\right)^{2}\right)
=∑s∈𝒮d0​(s)​(∑a∈𝒜πb​(a|s)​ρ​(s,a)2​B​(s,a,𝐧)2−(∑a∈𝒜πe​(a|s)​B​(s,a,𝐧))2)\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\left(\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{b}(a|s)\rho(s,a)^{2}B(s,a;\mathbf{n})^{2}-\left(\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{e}(a|s)B(s,a;\mathbf{n})\right)^{2}\right) (12)

We simplify the importance sampling weight term πb​(a|s)​ρ​(s,a)2\pi_{b}(a|s)\rho(s,a)^{2}:

πb​(a|s)​ρ​(s,a)2\displaystyle\pi_{b}(a|s)\rho(s,a)^{2} =πb​(a|s)​(πe​(a|s)πb​(a|s))2=πe​(a|s)2πb​(a|s)\displaystyle=\pi_{b}(a|s)\left(\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}\right)^{2}=\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}

Substituting this back into (12):

T3\displaystyle T_{3} =∑s∈𝒮d0(s)[∑a∈𝒜πe​(a|s)2πb​(a|s)B(s,a;𝐧)2\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\Bigg[\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}B(s,a;\mathbf{n})^{2}
−(∑a∈𝒜πe(a|s)B(s,a;𝐧))2]\displaystyle\quad-\left(\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{e}(a|s)B(s,a;\mathbf{n})\right)^{2}\Bigg] (13)

A.2 Term 4

The fourth term is given by:

T4=𝔼s∼d0[𝔼a∼πb(⋅|s)[(ρ(s,a)2−πe​(a|s)2πb​(a|s))Var𝒟(r^+(s,a))]]T_{4}=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{0}}\Bigg[\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{b}(\cdot|s)}\Bigg[\left(\rho(s,a)^{2}-\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}\right)\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal{D}}\left(\hat{r}^{+}(s,a)\right)\Bigg]\Bigg] (14)

First, for N⁡(s,a)>0N(s,a)>0, we calculate the reward-model variance Var𝒟⁡(r^+​(s,a))\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal{D}}\left(\hat{r}^{+}(s,a)\right). Using the independence of samples:

Var𝒟⁡(r^+​(s,a))\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal{D}}\left(\hat{r}^{+}(s,a)\right) =Var𝒟⁡(1N⁡(s,a)​(∑i=1nf​(s,a)ri+∑k=1K∑j=1nk​(s,a)gk,j))\displaystyle=\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal{D}}\left(\frac{1}{N(s,a)}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n_{f}(s,a)}r_{i}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{k}(s,a)}g_{k,j}\right)\right)
=1N​(s,a)2​(∑i=1nf​(s,a)Var⁡(ri)+∑k=1K∑j=1nk​(s,a)Var⁡(gk,j))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N(s,a)^{2}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n_{f}(s,a)}\operatorname{Var}(r_{i})+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{k}(s,a)}\operatorname{Var}(g_{k,j})\right)
=1N​(s,a)2​(nf​(s,a)​σr2​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​(σr2​(s,a)+Δgk​(s,a)))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N(s,a)^{2}}\left(n_{f}(s,a)\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)(\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a)+\Delta_{g_{k}}(s,a))\right)
=1N​(s,a)2​(nf​(s,a)​σr2​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​σr2​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​Δgk​(s,a))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N(s,a)^{2}}\left(n_{f}(s,a)\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\Delta_{g_{k}}(s,a)\right)
=1N​(s,a)2​((nf​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a))​σr2​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​Δgk​(s,a))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N(s,a)^{2}}\left(\left(n_{f}(s,a)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\right)\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\Delta_{g_{k}}(s,a)\right)
=1N​(s,a)2​(N⁡(s,a)​σr2​(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​Δgk​(s,a))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N(s,a)^{2}}\left(N(s,a)\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\Delta_{g_{k}}(s,a)\right)
=σr2​(s,a)N⁡(s,a)+∑k=1Knk​(s,a)​Δgk​(s,a)N​(s,a)2\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a)}{N(s,a)}+\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a)\Delta_{g_{k}}(s,a)}{N(s,a)^{2}} (15)

For N⁡(s,a)=0N(s,a)=0, the fixed default has variance zero, so Var𝒟⁡(r^+​(s,a))=W⁡(s,a,𝐧)\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal{D}}(\hat{r}^{+}(s,a))=W(s,a;\mathbf{n}) in both cases. Next, we substitute this variance into (14) and expand the expectations, evaluating divisions by πb​(a|s)\pi_{b}(a|s) only on its positive support:

T4\displaystyle T_{4} =∑s∈𝒮d0(s)∑a:πb​(a|s)>0πb(a|s)[(ρ(s,a)2−πe​(a|s)2πb​(a|s))Var𝒟(r^+(s,a))]\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\sum_{a:\pi_{b}(a|s)>0}\pi_{b}(a|s)\left[\left(\rho(s,a)^{2}-\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}\right)\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal{D}}\left(\hat{r}^{+}(s,a)\right)\right]
=∑s∈𝒮d0(s)∑a:πb​(a|s)>0[(πb(a|s)ρ(s,a)2−πb​(a|s)πb​(a|s)πe(a|s)2)Var𝒟(r^+(s,a))]\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\sum_{a:\pi_{b}(a|s)>0}\left[\left(\pi_{b}(a|s)\rho(s,a)^{2}-\frac{\pi_{b}(a|s)}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}\right)\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal{D}}\left(\hat{r}^{+}(s,a)\right)\right]
=∑s∈𝒮d0(s)∑a:πb​(a|s)>0[(πb(a|s)πe​(a|s)2πb​(a|s)2−πe(a|s)2)Var𝒟(r^+(s,a))]\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\sum_{a:\pi_{b}(a|s)>0}\left[\left(\pi_{b}(a|s)\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a|s)^{2}}-\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}\right)\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal{D}}\left(\hat{r}^{+}(s,a)\right)\right]
=∑s∈𝒮d0​(s)​∑a∈𝒜(πe​(a|s)2πb​(a|s)−πe​(a|s)2)​W​(s,a,𝐧)\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\left(\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}-\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}\right)W(s,a;\mathbf{n}) (16)

A.3 Objective Function

Let 𝐧={nj​(s,a)}s∈𝒮,a∈𝒜,j∈𝒦\mathbf{n}=\{n_{j}(s,a)\}_{s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A},j\in\mathcal{K}} denotes the set of decision variables. Combining (13) and (16), the objective function is:

J⁡(𝐧)\displaystyle J(\mathbf{n}) =∑s∈𝒮d0(s)[∑a∈𝒜πe​(a|s)2πb​(a|s)B(s,a;𝐧)2\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\Bigg[\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}B(s,a;\mathbf{n})^{2}
−(∑a∈𝒜πe​(a|s)​B​(s,a,𝐧))2\displaystyle\quad-\left(\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{e}(a|s)B(s,a;\mathbf{n})\right)^{2}
+∑a∈𝒜(πe​(a|s)2πb​(a|s)−πe(a|s)2)W(s,a;𝐧)].\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\left(\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}-\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}\right)W(s,a;\mathbf{n})\Bigg].

A.4 Theoretical bound for source-profile estimation error

The MSE decomposition above depends on source biases εgk\varepsilon_{g_{k}} and excess variances Δgk\Delta_{g_{k}}, which must often be estimated from pilot annotations. We first bound the resulting perturbation of JJ uniformly over feasible allocations, then translate this bound into the MSE guarantee in Theorem 2. Appendices E.4 and E.5 complement this analysis with finite-pilot evaluation and within-pair resampling.

Write x=(s,a)∈𝒳:=𝒮×𝒜x=(s,a)\in\mathcal{X}:=\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}, and define

fx:=nf​(s,a),mx​(𝐧):=∑k=1Knk​(s,a),Nx​(𝐧):=fx+mx​(𝐧).f_{x}:=n_{f}(s,a),\qquad m_{x}(\mathbf{n}):=\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(s,a),\qquad N_{x}(\mathbf{n}):=f_{x}+m_{x}(\mathbf{n}).

Let

θ:={(εgk​(x),Δgk​(x))}x,k\theta:=\left\{\bigl(\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(x),\Delta_{g_{k}}(x)\bigr)\right\}_{x,k}

and

θ^:={(ε^gk​(x),Δ^gk​(x))}x,k\hat{\theta}:=\left\{\bigl(\widehat{\varepsilon}_{g_{k}}(x),\widehat{\Delta}_{g_{k}}(x)\bigr)\right\}_{x,k}

denote the true and estimated source profiles, respectively. Define the uniform estimation errors

δε:=maxx,k⁡|ε^gk​(x)−εgk​(x)|,δΔ:=maxx,k⁡|Δ^gk​(x)−Δgk​(x)|.\delta_{\varepsilon}:=\max_{x,k}\left|\widehat{\varepsilon}_{g_{k}}(x)-\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(x)\right|,\qquad\delta_{\Delta}:=\max_{x,k}\left|\widehat{\Delta}_{g_{k}}(x)-\Delta_{g_{k}}(x)\right|.

To include the zero-factual-coverage case of Appendix B.8, define

Bx​(𝐧,θ):={∑k=1Knk​(x)​εgk​(x)Nx​(𝐧),Nx​(𝐧)>0,r0​(x)−μr​(x),Nx​(𝐧)=0.B_{x}(\mathbf{n};\theta):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}(x)\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(x)}{N_{x}(\mathbf{n})},&N_{x}(\mathbf{n})>0,\\[12.0pt] r_{0}(x)-\mu_{r}(x),&N_{x}(\mathbf{n})=0.\end{cases}

The same default r0​(x)r_{0}(x) is used under θ\theta and θ^\hat{\theta}. Let

βmax:=max{maxx,k|εgk(x)|,maxx:fx=0|r0(x)−μr(x)|}.\beta_{\max}:=\max\left\{\max_{x,k}|\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(x)|,\,\max_{x:f_{x}=0}|r_{0}(x)-\mu_{r}(x)|\right\}.

If factual rewards, source annotations, and the default value all lie in [0,R][0,R], then βmax≤R\beta_{\max}\leq R.

We next define two sensitivity constants. First,

A1:=∑s∈𝒮∑a∈𝒜α1​(s,a).A_{1}:=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\alpha_{1}(s,a).

For the excess-variance term, let MxM_{x} denote the maximum number of annotations that can feasibly be assigned to pair xx. Define

γx:=max0≤m≤Mxm∈ℤ⁡{m(fx+m)2,fx+m>0,0,fx=m=0.\gamma_{x}:=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq m\leq M_{x}\\ m\in\mathbb{Z}\end{subarray}}\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{m}{(f_{x}+m)^{2}},&f_{x}+m>0,\\[8.0pt] 0,&f_{x}=m=0.\end{cases} (17)

Define

A2:=∑x∈𝒳α3​(x)​γx.A_{2}:=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\alpha_{3}(x)\gamma_{x}.
Lemma 1 (Uniform perturbation of the allocation objective).

For every feasible allocation 𝐧∈ℱ\mathbf{n}\in\mathcal{F},

|J⁡(𝐧,θ^)−J⁡(𝐧,θ)|≤Φ⁡(δε,δΔ),\left|J(\mathbf{n};\hat{\theta})-J(\mathbf{n};\theta)\right|\leq\Phi(\delta_{\varepsilon},\delta_{\Delta}), (18)

where

Φ⁡(δε,δΔ):=A1​δε​(2​βmax+δε)+A2​δΔ.\Phi(\delta_{\varepsilon},\delta_{\Delta}):=A_{1}\delta_{\varepsilon}\left(2\beta_{\max}+\delta_{\varepsilon}\right)+A_{2}\delta_{\Delta}.
Proof.

Fix an allocation 𝐧\mathbf{n}, and define

Ux​(𝐧):=Bx​(𝐧,θ^)−Bx​(𝐧,θ).U_{x}(\mathbf{n}):=B_{x}(\mathbf{n};\hat{\theta})-B_{x}(\mathbf{n};\theta).

If Nx​(𝐧)>0N_{x}(\mathbf{n})>0, then

Ux​(𝐧)=∑knk​(x)​(ε^gk​(x)−εgk​(x))Nx​(𝐧),U_{x}(\mathbf{n})=\frac{\sum_{k}n_{k}(x)\left(\widehat{\varepsilon}_{g_{k}}(x)-\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(x)\right)}{N_{x}(\mathbf{n})},

and hence

|Ux​(𝐧)|≤mx​(𝐧)Nx​(𝐧)​δε≤δε.|U_{x}(\mathbf{n})|\leq\frac{m_{x}(\mathbf{n})}{N_{x}(\mathbf{n})}\delta_{\varepsilon}\leq\delta_{\varepsilon}. (19)

If Nx​(𝐧)=0N_{x}(\mathbf{n})=0, the same default is used under both parameter sets, so Ux​(𝐧)=0U_{x}(\mathbf{n})=0. Moreover,

|Bx​(𝐧,θ)|≤βmax.|B_{x}(\mathbf{n};\theta)|\leq\beta_{\max}.

For each context ss, define

Ms:=d0​(s)​[diag⁡(πe​(a∣s)2πb​(a∣s))a∈𝒜−𝝅e​(s)​𝝅e​(s)⊤],M_{s}:=d_{0}(s)\left[\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{\pi_{e}(a\mid s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a\mid s)}\right)_{a\in\mathcal{A}}-\boldsymbol{\pi}_{e}(s)\boldsymbol{\pi}_{e}(s)^{\top}\right],

where 𝝅e​(s):=(πe​(a∣s))a∈𝒜\boldsymbol{\pi}_{e}(s):=(\pi_{e}(a\mid s))_{a\in\mathcal{A}}. For any z∈ℝ|𝒜|z\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}|},

z⊤​Ms​z\displaystyle z^{\top}M_{s}z =d0​(s)​[∑aπe​(a∣s)2πb​(a∣s)​za2−(∑aπe​(a∣s)​za)2]\displaystyle=d_{0}(s)\left[\sum_{a}\frac{\pi_{e}(a\mid s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a\mid s)}z_{a}^{2}-\left(\sum_{a}\pi_{e}(a\mid s)z_{a}\right)^{2}\right]
=d0(s)Vara∼πb(⋅∣s)[πe​(a∣s)πb​(a∣s)za]≥0.\displaystyle=d_{0}(s)\operatorname{Var}_{a\sim\pi_{b}(\cdot\mid s)}\left[\frac{\pi_{e}(a\mid s)}{\pi_{b}(a\mid s)}z_{a}\right]\geq 0.

Therefore, Ms⪰0M_{s}\succeq 0.

Let

𝑩s:=(Bs,a​(𝐧,θ))a∈𝒜,𝑼s:=(Us,a​(𝐧))a∈𝒜.\boldsymbol{B}_{s}:=\bigl(B_{s,a}(\mathbf{n};\theta)\bigr)_{a\in\mathcal{A}},\qquad\boldsymbol{U}_{s}:=\bigl(U_{s,a}(\mathbf{n})\bigr)_{a\in\mathcal{A}}.

The combined bias term satisfies

J1​(𝐧,θ)−J2​(𝐧,θ)=∑s𝑩s⊤​Ms​𝑩s.J_{1}(\mathbf{n};\theta)-J_{2}(\mathbf{n};\theta)=\sum_{s}\boldsymbol{B}_{s}^{\top}M_{s}\boldsymbol{B}_{s}.

Using the seminorm induced by {Ms}s\{M_{s}\}_{s},

|[J1​(𝐧,θ^)−J2​(𝐧,θ^)]−[J1​(𝐧,θ)−J2​(𝐧,θ)]|\displaystyle\left|\bigl[J_{1}(\mathbf{n};\hat{\theta})-J_{2}(\mathbf{n};\hat{\theta})\bigr]-\bigl[J_{1}(\mathbf{n};\theta)-J_{2}(\mathbf{n};\theta)\bigr]\right| (20)
≤2​(∑s𝑩s⊤​Ms​𝑩s)1/2​(∑s𝑼s⊤​Ms​𝑼s)1/2+∑s𝑼s⊤​Ms​𝑼s.\displaystyle\leq 2\left(\sum_{s}\boldsymbol{B}_{s}^{\top}M_{s}\boldsymbol{B}_{s}\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{s}\boldsymbol{U}_{s}^{\top}M_{s}\boldsymbol{U}_{s}\right)^{1/2}+\sum_{s}\boldsymbol{U}_{s}^{\top}M_{s}\boldsymbol{U}_{s}.

Because the rank-one term subtracted in MsM_{s} is nonnegative,

∑s𝑩s⊤​Ms​𝑩s≤∑s,aα1​(s,a)​Bs,a2≤A1​βmax2,\sum_{s}\boldsymbol{B}_{s}^{\top}M_{s}\boldsymbol{B}_{s}\leq\sum_{s,a}\alpha_{1}(s,a)B_{s,a}^{2}\leq A_{1}\beta_{\max}^{2}, (21)

and, using (19),

∑s𝑼s⊤​Ms​𝑼s≤∑s,aα1​(s,a)​Us,a2≤A1​δε2.\sum_{s}\boldsymbol{U}_{s}^{\top}M_{s}\boldsymbol{U}_{s}\leq\sum_{s,a}\alpha_{1}(s,a)U_{s,a}^{2}\leq A_{1}\delta_{\varepsilon}^{2}. (22)

Substituting (21)–(22) into (20) gives

|[J1​(𝐧,θ^)−J2​(𝐧,θ^)]−[J1​(𝐧,θ)−J2​(𝐧,θ)]|≤A1​δε​(2​βmax+δε).\left|\bigl[J_{1}(\mathbf{n};\hat{\theta})-J_{2}(\mathbf{n};\hat{\theta})\bigr]-\bigl[J_{1}(\mathbf{n};\theta)-J_{2}(\mathbf{n};\theta)\bigr]\right|\leq A_{1}\delta_{\varepsilon}\left(2\beta_{\max}+\delta_{\varepsilon}\right). (23)

For the excess-variance term,

|J3​(𝐧,θ^)−J3​(𝐧,θ)|\displaystyle\left|J_{3}(\mathbf{n};\hat{\theta})-J_{3}(\mathbf{n};\theta)\right| ≤∑xα3​(x)​∑knk​(x)​|Δ^gk​(x)−Δgk​(x)|Nx​(𝐧)2\displaystyle\leq\sum_{x}\alpha_{3}(x)\frac{\sum_{k}n_{k}(x)\left|\widehat{\Delta}_{g_{k}}(x)-\Delta_{g_{k}}(x)\right|}{N_{x}(\mathbf{n})^{2}} (24)
≤δΔ​∑xα3​(x)​mx​(𝐧)(fx+mx​(𝐧))2\displaystyle\leq\delta_{\Delta}\sum_{x}\alpha_{3}(x)\frac{m_{x}(\mathbf{n})}{(f_{x}+m_{x}(\mathbf{n}))^{2}}
≤A2​δΔ,\displaystyle\leq A_{2}\delta_{\Delta},

where the ratio is defined as zero when fx=mx=0f_{x}=m_{x}=0, and the last inequality follows from (17). Combining (23) and (24) proves (18). ∎

Let

𝐧⋆∈arg⁡min𝐧∈ℱ⁡J⁡(𝐧,θ)\mathbf{n}^{\star}\in\arg\min_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathcal{F}}J(\mathbf{n};\theta)

be an optimal allocation under the population profiles. Let 𝐧^\widehat{\mathbf{n}} be the allocation returned by Algorithm 1 using θ^\hat{\theta}, and suppose that

J⁡(𝐧^,θ^)≤min𝐧∈ℱ⁡J⁡(𝐧,θ^)+ξalg,J(\widehat{\mathbf{n}};\hat{\theta})\leq\min_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathcal{F}}J(\mathbf{n};\hat{\theta})+\xi_{\mathrm{alg}}, (25)

where ξalg≥0\xi_{\mathrm{alg}}\geq 0 denotes the algorithmic suboptimality on the estimated objective.

Theorem 2 (Effect of source-profile estimation on MSE).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 1, assume that the pilot/allocation sample, the reward-model and annotation sample, and the OPE evaluation sample are independent. Conditional on the pilot, with factual counts, factual reward moments, and policy probabilities fixed, source-profile estimation introduces no additional OPE bias, and

MSE⁡(𝐧^)−MSE⁡(𝐧⋆)≤2​A1​δε​(2​βmax+δε)+2​A2​δΔ+ξalgN.\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat{\mathbf{n}})-\operatorname{MSE}(\mathbf{n}^{\star})\leq\frac{2A_{1}\delta_{\varepsilon}(2\beta_{\max}+\delta_{\varepsilon})+2A_{2}\delta_{\Delta}+\xi_{\mathrm{alg}}}{N}.
Proof.

Let

𝐧^⋆∈arg⁡min𝐧∈ℱ⁡J⁡(𝐧,θ^).\widehat{\mathbf{n}}^{\,\star}\in\arg\min_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathcal{F}}J(\mathbf{n};\hat{\theta}).

By adding and subtracting the estimated-objective values,

J⁡(𝐧^,θ)−J⁡(𝐧⋆,θ)\displaystyle J(\widehat{\mathbf{n}};\theta)-J(\mathbf{n}^{\star};\theta)
=[J⁡(𝐧^,θ)−J⁡(𝐧^,θ^)]+[J⁡(𝐧^,θ^)−J⁡(𝐧^⋆,θ^)]\displaystyle=\left[J(\widehat{\mathbf{n}};\theta)-J(\widehat{\mathbf{n}};\hat{\theta})\right]+\left[J(\widehat{\mathbf{n}};\hat{\theta})-J(\widehat{\mathbf{n}}^{\,\star};\hat{\theta})\right]
+[J⁡(𝐧^⋆,θ^)−J⁡(𝐧⋆,θ^)]+[J⁡(𝐧⋆,θ^)−J⁡(𝐧⋆,θ)].\displaystyle+\left[J(\widehat{\mathbf{n}}^{\,\star};\hat{\theta})-J(\mathbf{n}^{\star};\hat{\theta})\right]+\left[J(\mathbf{n}^{\star};\hat{\theta})-J(\mathbf{n}^{\star};\theta)\right].

By Lemma 1, the first and fourth terms are each at most Φ⁡(δε,δΔ)\Phi(\delta_{\varepsilon},\delta_{\Delta}). By (25), the second term is at most ξalg\xi_{\mathrm{alg}}, and the third term is nonpositive by the optimality of 𝐧^⋆\widehat{\mathbf{n}}^{\,\star} for the estimated objective. Hence,

J⁡(𝐧^,θ)−J⁡(𝐧⋆,θ)≤2​Φ​(δε,δΔ)+ξalg.J(\widehat{\mathbf{n}};\theta)-J(\mathbf{n}^{\star};\theta)\leq 2\Phi(\delta_{\varepsilon},\delta_{\Delta})+\xi_{\mathrm{alg}}. (26)

Using

Φ⁡(δε,δΔ)=A1​δε​(2​βmax+δε)+A2​δΔ,\Phi(\delta_{\varepsilon},\delta_{\Delta})=A_{1}\delta_{\varepsilon}\left(2\beta_{\max}+\delta_{\varepsilon}\right)+A_{2}\delta_{\Delta},

this becomes

J⁡(𝐧^,θ)−J⁡(𝐧⋆,θ)≤2​A1​δε​(2​βmax+δε)+2​A2​δΔ+ξalg.J(\widehat{\mathbf{n}};\theta)-J(\mathbf{n}^{\star};\theta)\leq 2A_{1}\delta_{\varepsilon}\left(2\beta_{\max}+\delta_{\varepsilon}\right)+2A_{2}\delta_{\Delta}+\xi_{\mathrm{alg}}. (27)

Under the stated data separation, DM+-IS is unbiased conditional on the pilot-selected allocation. Theorem 1 therefore gives

MSE⁡(𝐧)=C0+J⁡(𝐧,θ)N.\operatorname{MSE}(\mathbf{n})=C_{0}+\frac{J(\mathbf{n};\theta)}{N}.

Subtracting the MSE at 𝐧⋆\mathbf{n}^{\star} and applying (27) proves (4). ∎

Appendix B Threshold for Valuable Annotation for a single annotation source

In this appendix, we analyze, for a single annotation source, under what conditions adding counterfactual annotations improves or degrades the estimator variance. We begin with the simplest case (within a single context-action pair), then extend to actions within a single context, and finally consider arbitrary context-action pairs.

B.1 Setup and Notation

We consider a single annotation source (K=1K=1) and suppress the source index. For a fixed context-action pair (s,a)(s,a), let nf:=nf​(s,a)n_{f}:=n_{f}(s,a), ε:=εg​(s,a)\varepsilon:=\varepsilon_{g}(s,a), Δ:=Δg​(s,a)\Delta:=\Delta_{g}(s,a), σ2:=σr2​(s,a)\sigma^{2}:=\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a), and nn denote the number of annotations. We assume nf>0n_{f}>0 and α1>0\alpha_{1}>0 for the analysis below; the case nf=0n_{f}=0 is treated in Appendix B.8. The total sample size is N:=nf+nN:=n_{f}+n. Define the total annotation variance as σg2:=σ2+Δ\sigma_{g}^{2}:=\sigma^{2}+\Delta, and the policy-dependent ratio:

η⁡(s,a):=α3​(s,a)α1​(s,a)=πe​(a|s)2πb​(a|s)−πe​(a|s)2πe​(a|s)2πb​(a|s)=1−πb​(a|s).\eta(s,a):=\frac{\alpha_{3}(s,a)}{\alpha_{1}(s,a)}=\frac{\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}-\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}}{\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}}=1-\pi_{b}(a|s). (28)

This ratio satisfies 0≤η⁡(s,a)<10\leq\eta(s,a)<1 under the common support assumption πb​(a|s)>0\pi_{b}(a|s)>0, and measures how much the behavior policy under-covers action aa: small πb​(a|s)\pi_{b}(a|s) yields η\eta close to 1.

B.2 Bias Threshold for a Single Context-Action Pair

Ignoring the cross-action bias correction term (J2J_{2}) (since J2J_{2} couples all actions together, we will analysis it later in B.6), the contribution of a single (s,a)(s,a) to the objective is:

ϕ⁡(n):=α1​n2​ε2N2+α3​(σ2N+n​ΔN2)=α1​n2​ε2+α3​(nf​σ2+n​σg2)N2.\phi(n):=\alpha_{1}\frac{n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}{N^{2}}+\alpha_{3}\left(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{N}+\frac{n\Delta}{N^{2}}\right)=\frac{\alpha_{1}n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}\left(n_{f}\sigma^{2}+n\sigma_{g}^{2}\right)}{N^{2}}. (29)
Lemma 2 (Marginal Change for a single (s,a)).

The marginal change in the local objective when increasing the annotation count from nn to n+1n+1 is:

δ​ϕ​(n)\displaystyle\delta\phi(n) :=ϕ⁡(n+1)−ϕ⁡(n)\displaystyle:=\phi(n+1)-\phi(n) (30)
=α1​ε2​nf​((2​n+1)​N+n)+α3​σg2​(nf2−n⁡(n+1))−α3​nf​σ2​(2​N+1)N2​(N+1)2,\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}\bigl((2n+1)N+n\bigr)+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}\bigl(n_{f}^{2}-n(n+1)\bigr)-\alpha_{3}n_{f}\sigma^{2}(2N+1)}{N^{2}(N+1)^{2}},

where N=nf+nN=n_{f}+n.

Proof.

Write ϕ⁡(n)=P⁡(n)N2\phi(n)=\frac{P(n)}{N^{2}} where P⁡(n)=α1​n2​ε2+α3​nf​σ2+α3​n​σg2P(n)=\alpha_{1}n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}n_{f}\sigma^{2}+\alpha_{3}n\sigma_{g}^{2}. Then:

δ​ϕ​(n)=P⁡(n+1)⋅N2−P⁡(n)⋅(N+1)2N2​(N+1)2.\delta\phi(n)=\frac{P(n+1)\cdot N^{2}-P(n)\cdot(N+1)^{2}}{N^{2}(N+1)^{2}}. (31)

We decompose P⁡(n+1)=P⁡(n)+α1​(2​n+1)​ε2+α3​σg2P(n+1)=P(n)+\alpha_{1}(2n+1)\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2} and expand the numerator:

P⁡(n+1)​N2−P⁡(n)​(N+1)2\displaystyle P(n+1)N^{2}-P(n)(N+1)^{2}
=[P⁡(n)+α1​(2​n+1)​ε2+α3​σg2]​N2−P⁡(n)​(N+1)2\displaystyle=\bigl[P(n)+\alpha_{1}(2n+1)\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}\bigr]N^{2}-P(n)(N+1)^{2}
=P⁡(n)​[N2−(N+1)2]+[α1​(2​n+1)​ε2+α3​σg2]​N2\displaystyle=P(n)\bigl[N^{2}-(N+1)^{2}\bigr]+\bigl[\alpha_{1}(2n+1)\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}\bigr]N^{2}
=−P⁡(n)​(2​N+1)+[α1​(2​n+1)​ε2+α3​σg2]​N2.\displaystyle=-P(n)(2N+1)+\bigl[\alpha_{1}(2n+1)\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}\bigr]N^{2}. (32)

We evaluate each component in (32) separately. For the first term:

−P⁡(n)​(2​N+1)=−α1​n2​ε2​(2​N+1)−α3​nf​σ2​(2​N+1)−α3​n​σg2​(2​N+1).-P(n)(2N+1)=-\alpha_{1}n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}(2N+1)-\alpha_{3}n_{f}\sigma^{2}(2N+1)-\alpha_{3}n\sigma_{g}^{2}(2N+1). (33)

For the second term:

[α1​(2​n+1)​ε2+α3​σg2]​N2=α1​(2​n+1)​ε2​N2+α3​σg2​N2.\bigl[\alpha_{1}(2n+1)\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}\bigr]N^{2}=\alpha_{1}(2n+1)\varepsilon^{2}N^{2}+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}N^{2}. (34)

Collecting α1​ε2\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2} terms we get α1​ε2​[(2​n+1)​N2−n2​(2​N+1)]\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}\bigl[(2n+1)N^{2}-n^{2}(2N+1)\bigr].

We use the factorization (2​n+1)​N2−n2​(2​N+1)=[(2​n+1)​N+n]​[N−n]=nf​[(2​n+1)​N+n](2n+1)N^{2}-n^{2}(2N+1)=\bigl[(2n+1)N+n\bigr]\bigl[N-n\bigr]=n_{f}\bigl[(2n+1)N+n\bigr], which follows from the difference-of-products identity with N−n=nfN-n=n_{f}. Collecting α3​σg2\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2} terms:

α3​σg2​[N2−n⁡(2​N+1)]=α3​σg2​[nf2−n⁡(n+1)],\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}\bigl[N^{2}-n(2N+1)\bigr]=\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}\bigl[n_{f}^{2}-n(n+1)\bigr], (35)

where we expanded N2−n⁡(2​N+1)=(nf+n)2−2​n​(nf+n)−n=nf2+2​n​nf+n2−2​n​nf−2​n2−n=nf2−n2−nN^{2}-n(2N+1)=(n_{f}+n)^{2}-2n(n_{f}+n)-n=n_{f}^{2}+2nn_{f}+n^{2}-2nn_{f}-2n^{2}-n=n_{f}^{2}-n^{2}-n. The remaining term is −α3​nf​σ2​(2​N+1)-\alpha_{3}n_{f}\sigma^{2}(2N+1). Substitute (33) – (35) back into (31) yields Eq. (30). ∎

B.3 Proof of Theorem 3 (First Annotation Threshold)

Theorem 3.

With η⁡(s,a)\eta(s,a) in (28), the first annotation (n=0→1n=0\to 1) does not increase the local objective (29), i.e., δ​ϕ​(0)≤0\delta\phi(0)\leq 0, if and only if

ε2​(s,a)≤η⁡(s,a)​((nf​(s,a)+1)​σ2​(s,a)nf​(s,a)−Δ⁡(s,a)).\varepsilon^{2}(s,a)\leq\eta(s,a)\!\left(\frac{(n_{f}(s,a)+1)\sigma^{2}(s,a)}{n_{f}(s,a)}-\Delta(s,a)\right). (36)

Equality in (36) leaves the local objective unchanged, whereas strict inequality gives a strict decrease. In particular, if Δ⁡(s,a)≥(nf​(s,a)+1)​σ2/nf​(s,a)\Delta(s,a)\geq(n_{f}(s,a)+1)\sigma^{2}/n_{f}(s,a), then δ​ϕ​(0)>0\delta\phi(0)>0 for every (s,a) with ε⁡(s,a)≠0\varepsilon(s,a)\neq 0.

Proof.

Substituting n=0n=0 and N=nfN=n_{f} into Eq. (30):

δ​ϕ​(0)\displaystyle\delta\phi(0) =α1​ε2​nf⋅nf+α3​σg2⋅nf2−α3​nf​σ2​(2​nf+1)nf2​(nf+1)2\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}\cdot n_{f}+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}\cdot n_{f}^{2}-\alpha_{3}n_{f}\sigma^{2}(2n_{f}+1)}{n_{f}^{2}(n_{f}+1)^{2}}
=nf​[α1​ε2​nf+α3​nf​σg2−α3​(2​nf+1)​σ2]nf2​(nf+1)2\displaystyle=\frac{n_{f}\bigl[\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}+\alpha_{3}n_{f}\sigma_{g}^{2}-\alpha_{3}(2n_{f}+1)\sigma^{2}\bigr]}{n_{f}^{2}(n_{f}+1)^{2}}
=α1​ε2​nf+α3​[nf​(σ2+Δ)−(2​nf+1)​σ2]nf​(nf+1)2\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}+\alpha_{3}\bigl[n_{f}(\sigma^{2}+\Delta)-(2n_{f}+1)\sigma^{2}\bigr]}{n_{f}(n_{f}+1)^{2}}
=α1​ε2​nf+α3​[nf​Δ−(nf+1)​σ2]nf​(nf+1)2.\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}+\alpha_{3}\bigl[n_{f}\Delta-(n_{f}+1)\sigma^{2}\bigr]}{n_{f}(n_{f}+1)^{2}}. (37)

Because nf>0n_{f}>0 and α1>0\alpha_{1}>0, the condition δ​ϕ​(0)≤0\delta\phi(0)\leq 0 is equivalent to

α1​ε2​nf\displaystyle\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f} ≤α3​[(nf+1)​σ2−nf​Δ],\displaystyle\leq\alpha_{3}\bigl[(n_{f}+1)\sigma^{2}-n_{f}\Delta\bigr],
ε2\displaystyle\varepsilon^{2} ≤α3α1​((nf+1)​σ2nf−Δ)=η⁡(s,a)​((nf+1)​σ2nf−Δ).\displaystyle\leq\frac{\alpha_{3}}{\alpha_{1}}\left(\frac{(n_{f}+1)\sigma^{2}}{n_{f}}-\Delta\right)=\eta(s,a)\left(\frac{(n_{f}+1)\sigma^{2}}{n_{f}}-\Delta\right).

The same equivalence holds with either equality or strict inequality throughout. When Δ≥(nf+1)​σ2/nf\Delta\geq(n_{f}+1)\sigma^{2}/n_{f} and ε≠0\varepsilon\neq 0, the right-hand side is nonpositive while ε2>0\varepsilon^{2}>0, so (37) gives δ​ϕ​(0)>0\delta\phi(0)>0. ∎

B.4 Proof of Theorem 4 (Four Regimes of Annotation Value)

Lemma 3 (Continuous Critical Point n∗n^{*}).

Treating nn as a continuous variable, the derivative of ϕ\phi is:

ϕ′​(n)=(2​α1​ε2​nf−α3​σg2)​n+α3​nf​(Δ−σ2)(nf+n)3.\phi^{\prime}(n)=\frac{(2\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}-\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2})\,n+\alpha_{3}n_{f}(\Delta-\sigma^{2})}{(n_{f}+n)^{3}}. (38)

If 2​α1​ε2​nf≠α3​σg22\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}\neq\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}, the only possible critical point is

n∗=α3​nf​(σ2−Δ)2​α1​ε2​nf−α3​σg2=η​nf​(σ2−Δ)2​ε2​nf−η​σg2.n^{*}=\frac{\alpha_{3}n_{f}(\sigma^{2}-\Delta)}{2\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}-\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}}=\frac{\eta\,n_{f}(\sigma^{2}-\Delta)}{2\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}-\eta\,\sigma_{g}^{2}}. (39)

It is an interior critical point exactly when n∗>0n^{*}>0. If 2​α1​ε2​nf=α3​σg22\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}=\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}, there is no interior critical point unless α3​(Δ−σ2)=0\alpha_{3}(\Delta-\sigma^{2})=0, in which case ϕ\phi is constant. Furthermore, ϕ⁡(n)→α1​ε2\phi(n)\to\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2} as n→∞n\to\infty.

Proof.

From Eq. (29), ϕ⁡(n)=P⁡(n)/N2\phi(n)=P(n)/N^{2} where P⁡(n)=α1​n2​ε2+α3​nf​σ2+α3​n​σg2P(n)=\alpha_{1}n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}n_{f}\sigma^{2}+\alpha_{3}n\sigma_{g}^{2} and N=nf+nN=n_{f}+n. By the quotient rule:

ϕ′​(n)\displaystyle\phi^{\prime}(n) =P′​(n)​N2−P⁡(n)⋅2​NN4=P′​(n)​N−2​P​(n)N3,\displaystyle=\frac{P^{\prime}(n)N^{2}-P(n)\cdot 2N}{N^{4}}=\frac{P^{\prime}(n)N-2P(n)}{N^{3}}, (40)

where P′​(n)=2​α1​n​ε2+α3​σg2P^{\prime}(n)=2\alpha_{1}n\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}. Expanding the numerator:

(2​α1​n​ε2+α3​σg2)​(nf+n)−2​(α1​n2​ε2+α3​nf​σ2+α3​n​σg2)\displaystyle(2\alpha_{1}n\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2})(n_{f}+n)-2(\alpha_{1}n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}n_{f}\sigma^{2}+\alpha_{3}n\sigma_{g}^{2})
=2​α1​n​ε2​nf+2​α1​n2​ε2+α3​σg2​nf+α3​σg2​n−2​α1​n2​ε2−2​α3​nf​σ2−2​α3​n​σg2\displaystyle=2\alpha_{1}n\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}+2\alpha_{1}n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}n_{f}+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}n-2\alpha_{1}n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}-2\alpha_{3}n_{f}\sigma^{2}-2\alpha_{3}n\sigma_{g}^{2}
=2​α1​ε2​nf​n+α3​nf​(σg2−2​σ2)−α3​σg2​n\displaystyle=2\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}\,n+\alpha_{3}n_{f}(\sigma_{g}^{2}-2\sigma^{2})-\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}n
=(2​α1​ε2​nf−α3​σg2)​n+α3​nf​(Δ−σ2),\displaystyle=(2\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}-\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2})\,n+\alpha_{3}n_{f}(\Delta-\sigma^{2}), (41)

where we used σg2−2​σ2=Δ−σ2\sigma_{g}^{2}-2\sigma^{2}=\Delta-\sigma^{2}. When its slope is nonzero, setting the numerator to zero yields Eq. (39), with an interior solution exactly when n∗>0n^{*}>0. When the slope is zero, the numerator is the constant α3​nf​(Δ−σ2)\alpha_{3}n_{f}(\Delta-\sigma^{2}), so the derivative either never vanishes or is identically zero.

For the limit, divide numerator and denominator of ϕ⁡(n)\phi(n) by n2n^{2}:

ϕ⁡(n)=α1​ε2+α3​nf​σ2/n2+α3​σg2/n(nf/n+1)2→n→∞α1​ε2.∎\phi(n)=\frac{\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}n_{f}\sigma^{2}/n^{2}+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}/n}{(n_{f}/n+1)^{2}}\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}.\qed

Define the slope and intercept of the numerator in Eq. (38) as:

𝔞:=2​α1​ε2​nf−α3​σg2,𝔟:=α3​nf​(Δ−σ2).\mathfrak{a}:=2\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}-\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2},\qquad\mathfrak{b}:=\alpha_{3}n_{f}(\Delta-\sigma^{2}). (42)
Theorem 4 (Four Regimes of Annotation Value).

In all cases, ϕ⁡(n)→α1​ε2\phi(n)\to\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2} as n→∞n\to\infty. When 𝔞=𝔟=0\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{b}=0, ϕ\phi is constant; otherwise, it falls into four regimes:

  1. (I)

    If 𝔞≥0\mathfrak{a}\geq 0 and 𝔟≥0\mathfrak{b}\geq 0, then ϕ\phi is increasing, so annotations are locally harmful.

  2. (II)

    If 𝔞>0\mathfrak{a}>0 and 𝔟<0\mathfrak{b}<0, then ϕ\phi decreases and then increases, with unique continuous minimizer n∗=η​nf​(σ2−Δ)/(2​ε2​nf−η​σg2)n^{*}=\eta n_{f}(\sigma^{2}-\Delta)/(2\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}-\eta\sigma_{g}^{2}).

  3. (III)

    If 𝔞≤0\mathfrak{a}\leq 0 and 𝔟≤0\mathfrak{b}\leq 0, then ϕ\phi is decreasing, so each additional annotation locally reduces the objective.

  4. (IV)

    If 𝔞<0\mathfrak{a}<0 and 𝔟>0\mathfrak{b}>0, then ϕ\phi first increases and then decreases, with unique continuous maximizer n¯=η​nf​(Δ−σ2)/(η​σg2−2​ε2​nf)\bar{n}=\eta n_{f}(\Delta-\sigma^{2})/(\eta\sigma_{g}^{2}-2\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}). In this regime, a strict improvement over no annotation is possible if and only if ε2<η​σ2/nf\varepsilon^{2}<\eta\sigma^{2}/n_{f}.

Proof.

The numerator of ϕ′​(n)\phi^{\prime}(n) is 𝔞​n+𝔟\mathfrak{a}n+\mathfrak{b}, and the denominator (nf+n)3>0(n_{f}+n)^{3}>0 for all n≥0n\geq 0. Hence sign⁡(ϕ′​(n))=sign⁡(𝔞​n+𝔟)\operatorname{sign}(\phi^{\prime}(n))=\operatorname{sign}(\mathfrak{a}n+\mathfrak{b}) for n>0n>0. If 𝔞=𝔟=0\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{b}=0, then ϕ′​(n)=0\phi^{\prime}(n)=0 for every n≥0n\geq 0, so ϕ⁡(n)=ϕ⁡(0)=α1​ε2\phi(n)=\phi(0)=\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2} throughout. When η=0\eta=0, we have α3=0\alpha_{3}=0 and ϕ⁡(n)=α1​ε2​n2/(nf+n)2\phi(n)=\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n^{2}/(n_{f}+n)^{2}; thus ε≠0\varepsilon\neq 0 gives Regime (I), while ε=0\varepsilon=0 gives the constant zero objective, regardless of Δ\Delta. For η>0\eta>0, equivalently α3>0\alpha_{3}>0, we translate the four sign patterns into the source conditions in Table 1, excluding the constant case.

Regime (I): 𝔞≥0\mathfrak{a}\geq 0 and 𝔟≥0\mathfrak{b}\geq 0 (not both zero). Then 𝔞​n+𝔟>0\mathfrak{a}n+\mathfrak{b}>0 for all n>0n>0, so ϕ′​(n)>0\phi^{\prime}(n)>0. The condition 𝔟≥0\mathfrak{b}\geq 0 is Δ≥σ2\Delta\geq\sigma^{2}. The condition 𝔞≥0\mathfrak{a}\geq 0 is 2​α1​ε2​nf≥α3​σg22\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}\geq\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}, which gives ε2≥α3​σg22​α1​nf=η​σg22​nf\varepsilon^{2}\geq\frac{\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}}{2\alpha_{1}n_{f}}=\frac{\eta\sigma_{g}^{2}}{2n_{f}}.

Regime (II): 𝔞>0\mathfrak{a}>0 and 𝔟<0\mathfrak{b}<0. The affine function 𝔞​n+𝔟\mathfrak{a}n+\mathfrak{b} starts negative at n=0n=0 and increases, crossing zero at n∗=−𝔟/𝔞>0n^{*}=-\mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{a}>0. For n<n∗n<n^{*}, ϕ′​(n)<0\phi^{\prime}(n)<0 (decreasing); for n>n∗n>n^{*}, ϕ′​(n)>0\phi^{\prime}(n)>0 (increasing). The condition 𝔟<0\mathfrak{b}<0 is Δ<σ2\Delta<\sigma^{2}. The condition 𝔞>0\mathfrak{a}>0 gives ε2>η​σg22​nf\varepsilon^{2}>\frac{\eta\sigma_{g}^{2}}{2n_{f}}.

Regime (III): 𝔞≤0,𝔟≤0\mathfrak{a}\leq 0,\mathfrak{b}\leq 0 (not both zero) gives 𝔞​n+𝔟≤0\mathfrak{a}n+\mathfrak{b}\leq 0 for all n>0n>0, with strict inequality whenever at least one of 𝔞,𝔟\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b} is strictly negative. The conditions are Δ≤σ2\Delta\leq\sigma^{2} and ε2≤η​σg2/(2​nf)\varepsilon^{2}\leq\eta\sigma_{g}^{2}/(2n_{f}), with at least one inequality strict. In particular, Δ=σ2\Delta=\sigma^{2} is included when ε2<η​σ2/nf\varepsilon^{2}<\eta\sigma^{2}/n_{f}; equality in both conditions gives the constant case already treated.

Regime (IV): The sign transition is reversed: 𝔟>0\mathfrak{b}>0 gives ϕ′​(0+)>0\phi^{\prime}(0^{+})>0, and 𝔞<0\mathfrak{a}<0 forces a sign change at the maximizer n¯=−𝔟/𝔞>0\bar{n}=-\mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{a}>0 stated in the theorem. For the sub-case analysis, we examine ϕ⁡(n)−ϕ⁡(0)\phi(n)-\phi(0). The function increases up to n¯\bar{n}, then decreases toward α1​ε2\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}.

Sub-case (IVa): α1​ε2<ϕ⁡(0)\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}<\phi(0). Because limn→∞ϕ⁡(n)<ϕ⁡(0)\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi(n)<\phi(0), there is a finite T>n¯T>\bar{n} with ϕ⁡(T)<ϕ⁡(0)\phi(T)<\phi(0). The intermediate value theorem on [n¯,T][\bar{n},T], together with ϕ⁡(n¯)>ϕ⁡(0)\phi(\bar{n})>\phi(0) and strict decrease after n¯\bar{n}, gives a unique break-even count nbe>n¯n_{\mathrm{be}}>\bar{n} satisfying ϕ⁡(nbe)=ϕ⁡(0)\phi(n_{\mathrm{be}})=\phi(0). Consequently, ϕ⁡(n)<ϕ⁡(0)\phi(n)<\phi(0) exactly when n>nben>n_{\mathrm{be}}; under a finite capacity, this improvement is attainable only if such a count is feasible.

Sub-case (IVb): α1​ε2≥ϕ⁡(0)\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}\geq\phi(0). We show ϕ⁡(n)≥ϕ⁡(0)\phi(n)\geq\phi(0) for all n≥0n\geq 0. Since ϕ\phi is increasing on (0,n¯)(0,\bar{n}), we have ϕ⁡(n)>ϕ⁡(0)\phi(n)>\phi(0) for n∈(0,n¯]n\in(0,\bar{n}]. On (n¯,∞)(\bar{n},\infty), ϕ\phi is strictly decreasing toward α1​ε2≥ϕ⁡(0)\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}\geq\phi(0). Thus ϕ⁡(n)>α1​ε2≥ϕ⁡(0)\phi(n)>\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}\geq\phi(0) for every n>n¯n>\bar{n}, proving the claim, including the boundary case α1​ε2=ϕ⁡(0)\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}=\phi(0).

The sub-case condition α1​ε2≶ϕ⁡(0)=α3​σ2/nf\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}\lessgtr\phi(0)=\alpha_{3}\sigma^{2}/n_{f} translates to ε2≶η​σ2/nf\varepsilon^{2}\lessgtr\eta\sigma^{2}/n_{f}. ∎

Integer counts in Regime (II).

For the local problem with feasible counts n∈{0,…,U}n\in\{0,\ldots,U\}, where UU is a nonnegative integer, it suffices to compare ϕ\phi at min⁡{⌊n∗⌋,U}\min\{\lfloor n^{*}\rfloor,U\} and min⁡{⌈n∗⌉,U}\min\{\lceil n^{*}\rceil,U\}. If n∗≤Un^{*}\leq U, monotonicity on each side of n∗n^{*} implies that every feasible integer has an objective value at least as large as that at ⌊n∗⌋\lfloor n^{*}\rfloor or ⌈n∗⌉\lceil n^{*}\rceil. If n∗>Un^{*}>U, ϕ\phi decreases throughout [0,U][0,U], so both capped candidates equal the optimum UU. When the candidates coincide, including U=0U=0 or integer n∗n^{*}, only one evaluation is needed; if their objective values tie, either is optimal.

B.5 Asymptotic Behavior and Bias Floor

Corollary 1 (Diminishing Marginal Returns).

In all regimes, the marginal effect of annotation vanishes asymptotically:

|ϕ′​(n)|=|𝔞​n+𝔟|(nf+n)3=O⁡(1n2)as ​n→∞.|\phi^{\prime}(n)|=\frac{|\mathfrak{a}\,n+\mathfrak{b}|}{(n_{f}+n)^{3}}=O\!\left(\frac{1}{n^{2}}\right)\quad\text{as }n\to\infty. (43)

In Regime (II), annotations beyond n∗n^{*} increase ϕ\phi, with marginal cost of magnitude O⁡(1/n2)O(1/n^{2}). In Regime (III), and in Regime (IV) beyond the maximizer n¯\bar{n}, annotations decrease ϕ\phi, with marginal benefit of magnitude O⁡(1/n2)O(1/n^{2}). The discrete marginal change δ​ϕ​(n)=ϕ⁡(n+1)−ϕ⁡(n)\delta\phi(n)=\phi(n+1)-\phi(n) also has magnitude O⁡(1/n2)O(1/n^{2}).

Proof.

For n≥1n\geq 1, |𝔞​n+𝔟|≤(|𝔞|+|𝔟|)​n|\mathfrak{a}n+\mathfrak{b}|\leq(|\mathfrak{a}|+|\mathfrak{b}|)n and (nf+n)3≥n3(n_{f}+n)^{3}\geq n^{3}, so |ϕ′​(n)|≤(|𝔞|+|𝔟|)/n2|\phi^{\prime}(n)|\leq(|\mathfrak{a}|+|\mathfrak{b}|)/n^{2}. The signs follow from Theorem 4: ϕ′>0\phi^{\prime}>0 after the minimum in Regime (II), whereas ϕ′<0\phi^{\prime}<0 throughout Regime (III) and after the maximum in Regime (IV). For integer n≥1n\geq 1, the mean value theorem gives δ​ϕ​(n)=ϕ′​(ξn)\delta\phi(n)=\phi^{\prime}(\xi_{n}) for some ξn∈(n,n+1)\xi_{n}\in(n,n+1), yielding the same bound on its magnitude. ∎

Corollary 2 (Irreducible Bias Floor).

Regardless of regime, limn→∞ϕ⁡(n)=α1​ε2\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi(n)=\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}. The asymptotic reduction relative to no annotation is

ϕ⁡(0)−α1​ε2=α1nf​[η​σ2−nf​ε2].\phi(0)-\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}=\frac{\alpha_{1}}{n_{f}}\bigl[\eta\,\sigma^{2}-n_{f}\varepsilon^{2}\bigr]. (44)

This quantity is positive if and only if ε2<η​σ2nf\varepsilon^{2}<\frac{\eta\,\sigma^{2}}{n_{f}}, which is exactly the condition separating sub-cases (IVa) from (IVb). The condition holds throughout the nonconstant Regime (III), including the boundary Δ=σ2\Delta=\sigma^{2}. In Regime (II), the asymptotic floor may exceed ϕ⁡(0)\phi(0) when ε\varepsilon is large; however, the local optimum ϕ⁡(n∗)\phi(n^{*}) always satisfies ϕ⁡(n∗)<ϕ⁡(0)\phi(n^{*})<\phi(0) since ϕ′​(0+)<0\phi^{\prime}(0^{+})<0 guarantees initial descent.

Proof.

The limit and the formula follow from Lemma 3. Regime (III) requires η>0\eta>0, because η=0\eta=0 gives either Regime (I) or the constant case. If Δ<σ2\Delta<\sigma^{2}, then ε2≤η​σg2/(2​nf)<η​σ2/nf\varepsilon^{2}\leq\eta\sigma_{g}^{2}/(2n_{f})<\eta\sigma^{2}/n_{f}. If Δ=σ2\Delta=\sigma^{2}, then 𝔟=0\mathfrak{b}=0 and the nonconstant Regime (III) requires 𝔞<0\mathfrak{a}<0, which gives ε2<η​σ2/nf\varepsilon^{2}<\eta\sigma^{2}/n_{f} directly. In the excluded constant case, ϕ⁡(0)=α1​ε2\phi(0)=\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}, so the asymptotic reduction is zero. For Regime (II): 𝔟<0\mathfrak{b}<0 implies ϕ′​(0+)=𝔟/nf3<0\phi^{\prime}(0^{+})=\mathfrak{b}/n_{f}^{3}<0, so ϕ\phi is initially decreasing. Since n∗n^{*} is the unique minimum of ϕ\phi on (0,∞)(0,\infty), continuity gives ϕ⁡(n∗)<ϕ⁡(ϵ)<ϕ⁡(0)\phi(n^{*})<\phi(\epsilon)<\phi(0) for sufficiently small ϵ>0\epsilon>0. ∎

B.6 Cross-Action Coupling within a Context

When multiple actions are annotated within the same context, the marginal value of an annotation also depends on how it changes the aggregate bias in J2J_{2}. We compute this correction to identify when it strengthens or weakens the local benefit derived above.

Lemma 4 (Marginal change including J2J_{2}).

Consider adding one annotation (from nn to n+1n+1) for action aa at context ss. The total marginal change in the objective, including the bias correction term J2J_{2}, is:

δ​J​(n)=δ​ϕ​(n)−δ​J2​(n),\delta J(n)=\delta\phi(n)-\delta J_{2}(n), (45)

where δ​ϕ​(n)\delta\phi(n) is the local change from Lemma 2 and:

δ​J2​(n)=d0​(s)​[2​ℬs⋅πe​(a|s)​nf​εN⁡(N+1)+(πe​(a|s)​nf​εN⁡(N+1))2],\delta J_{2}(n)=d_{0}(s)\left[2\mathcal{B}_{s}\cdot\pi_{e}(a|s)\frac{n_{f}\varepsilon}{N(N+1)}+\left(\pi_{e}(a|s)\frac{n_{f}\varepsilon}{N(N+1)}\right)^{2}\right], (46)

with ℬs:=∑a′∈𝒜πe​(a′|s)​B​(s,a′,𝐧)\mathcal{B}_{s}:=\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{e}(a^{\prime}|s)B(s,a^{\prime};\mathbf{n}) being the current weighted bias accumulation, including default-model biases at pairs with N⁡(s,a′)=0N(s,a^{\prime})=0.

Proof.

The bias accumulation for context ss changes from ℬs\mathcal{B}_{s} to ℬs′=ℬs+πe​(a|s)​δ​B​(s,a)\mathcal{B}_{s}^{\prime}=\mathcal{B}_{s}+\pi_{e}(a|s)\,\delta B(s,a), where:

δ​B​(s,a)\displaystyle\delta B(s,a) :=(n+1)​εN+1−n​εN=ε​(n+1)​N−n⁡(N+1)N⁡(N+1)=nf​εN⁡(N+1).\displaystyle:=\frac{(n+1)\varepsilon}{N+1}-\frac{n\varepsilon}{N}=\varepsilon\frac{(n+1)N-n(N+1)}{N(N+1)}=\frac{n_{f}\varepsilon}{N(N+1)}. (47)

Therefore:

δ​J2​(n)\displaystyle\delta J_{2}(n) =d0​(s)​[(ℬs′)2−ℬs2]=d0​(s)​[2​ℬs⋅πe​(a|s)​δ​B+(πe​(a|s)​δ​B)2].\displaystyle=d_{0}(s)\bigl[(\mathcal{B}_{s}^{\prime})^{2}-\mathcal{B}_{s}^{2}\bigr]=d_{0}(s)\bigl[2\mathcal{B}_{s}\cdot\pi_{e}(a|s)\,\delta B+\bigl(\pi_{e}(a|s)\,\delta B\bigr)^{2}\bigr]. (48)

Since −J2-J_{2} appears in the objective, the total change is δ​J=δ​ϕ−δ​J2\delta J=\delta\phi-\delta J_{2}. ∎

Remark 1 (Sign of δ​J2\delta J_{2}).

The quadratic term in (46) is non-negative, but the linear term 2​d0​(s)​ℬs​πe​(a|s)​nf​ε/[N⁡(N+1)]2d_{0}(s)\mathcal{B}_{s}\,\pi_{e}(a|s)\,n_{f}\varepsilon/[N(N+1)] has the sign of ℬs⋅ε\mathcal{B}_{s}\cdot\varepsilon. Therefore δ​J​(n)\delta J(n) may be either smaller or larger than δ​ϕ​(n)\delta\phi(n) depending on whether the new bias correlates with or opposes the existing aggregate bias ℬs\mathcal{B}_{s}. This is exactly why allocation decisions cannot be made independently across actions.

Theorem 5 (Threshold including bias correction).

Assume α3>0\alpha_{3}>0. If the aggregate bias before the first annotation for action aa is ℬs(0)=0\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(0)}=0, then this annotation does not increase the objective (δ​J​(0)≤0\delta J(0)\leq 0) if and only if

ε2≤(nf+1)​σ2nf−Δ.\varepsilon^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{(n_{f}+1)\sigma^{2}}{n_{f}}-\Delta. (49)

Equality in (49) gives δ​J​(0)=0\delta J(0)=0, whereas strict inequality gives δ​J​(0)<0\delta J(0)<0. When the right-hand side of (49) is positive, including J2J_{2} multiplies the allowable squared bias from Theorem 3 by 1/η>11/\eta>1. For general ℬs(0)≠0\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(0)}\neq 0, the threshold becomes

α3​ε2≤α3​[(nf+1)​σ2−nf​Δ]nf+2​d0​(s)​ℬs(0)​πe​(a|s)​(nf+1)​ε,\alpha_{3}\,\varepsilon^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{\alpha_{3}\bigl[(n_{f}+1)\sigma^{2}-n_{f}\Delta\bigr]}{n_{f}}+2d_{0}(s)\,\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(0)}\,\pi_{e}(a|s)\,(n_{f}+1)\,\varepsilon, (50)

which couples the allowable bias of action aa to the existing aggregate bias of context ss.

Proof.

The condition δ​J​(0)≤0\delta J(0)\leq 0 is equivalent to δ​ϕ​(0)≤δ​J2​(0)\delta\phi(0)\leq\delta J_{2}(0). At n=0n=0, N=nfN=n_{f} and the increment δ​B​(s,a)=ε/(nf+1)\delta B(s,a)=\varepsilon/(n_{f}+1) (Eq. 47). Substituting δ​ϕ​(0)\delta\phi(0) from Eq. (37) and δ​J2​(0)\delta J_{2}(0) from Eq. (48):

α1​ε2​nf+α3​(nf​Δ−(nf+1)​σ2)nf​(nf+1)2≤d0​(s)​ 2​ℬs(0)​πe​(a|s)​εnf+1+d0​(s)​πe​(a|s)2​ε2(nf+1)2.\frac{\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}n_{f}+\alpha_{3}(n_{f}\Delta-(n_{f}+1)\sigma^{2})}{n_{f}(n_{f}+1)^{2}}\leq\frac{d_{0}(s)\,2\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(0)}\pi_{e}(a|s)\,\varepsilon}{n_{f}+1}+\frac{d_{0}(s)\,\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}\,\varepsilon^{2}}{(n_{f}+1)^{2}}. (51)

Multiplying both sides by (nf+1)2(n_{f}+1)^{2} and rearranging, we collect ε2\varepsilon^{2} terms:

(α1−d0​(s)​πe​(a|s)2)​ε2≤α3​((nf+1)​σ2−nf​Δ)nf+2​d0​(s)​ℬs(0)​πe​(a|s)​(nf+1)​ε.\bigl(\alpha_{1}-d_{0}(s)\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}\bigr)\varepsilon^{2}\leq\frac{\alpha_{3}\bigl((n_{f}+1)\sigma^{2}-n_{f}\Delta\bigr)}{n_{f}}+2d_{0}(s)\,\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(0)}\,\pi_{e}(a|s)\,(n_{f}+1)\,\varepsilon. (52)

The key identity is:

α1−d0​(s)​πe​(a|s)2=d0​(s)​πe​(a|s)2​(1πb​(a|s)−1)=α3.\alpha_{1}-d_{0}(s)\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}=d_{0}(s)\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}\!\left(\frac{1}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}-1\right)=\alpha_{3}. (53)

Substitute Eq. (53) into LHS of Eq. (52) yields Eq. (50). Setting ℬs(0)=0\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(0)}=0 and dividing by α3>0\alpha_{3}>0 gives Eq. (49). All transformations preserve equality and strict inequality, proving the corresponding statements for δ​J​(0)=0\delta J(0)=0 and δ​J​(0)<0\delta J(0)<0. ∎

B.7 Extension to Arbitrary Context-Action Pairs

In (2), each aggregate bias ℬs\mathcal{B}_{s} depends only on allocations within context ss. Thus the objective is additive across contexts: J⁡(𝐧)=∑s∈𝒮Js​(𝐧s)J(\mathbf{n})=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}J_{s}(\mathbf{n}_{s}), where 𝐧s:={nk(s,a):a∈𝒜,k∈𝒦}\mathbf{n}_{s}:=\{n_{k}(s,a):a\in\mathcal{A},\ k\in\mathcal{K}\} and JsJ_{s} contains that context’s terms. The shared budget in (3) nevertheless couples the feasible choices across contexts.

The four regimes in Theorem 4 and the diminishing marginal effects in Corollary 1 describe the local objective ϕ\phi, which omits J2J_{2}. They do not directly characterize the coupled context objective JsJ_{s}. For a single annotation with other allocations held fixed, Theorem 5 gives the full first-annotation condition through the current aggregate bias. Joint allocation must therefore account for both within-context bias coupling and the shared budget, as in §6.

B.8 The Case nf​(s,a)=0n_{f}(s,a)=0

When nf​(s,a)=0n_{f}(s,a)=0, the fitting data contain no observations for the pair (s,a)(s,a). This can occur even when πb​(a|s)>0\pi_{b}(a|s)>0, so an empty fitting cell does not by itself violate common support. The formulas in Theorem 4 require nf>0n_{f}>0. We treat this case separately.

B.8.1 πb​(a|s)>0\pi_{b}(a|s)>0 but nf​(s,a)=0n_{f}(s,a)=0

We retain the single-source setting and consider pairs with α1>0\alpha_{1}>0; if α1=0\alpha_{1}=0, then α3=0\alpha_{3}=0 and the local objective is identically zero. When no annotations have been acquired, N⁡(s,a)=0N(s,a)=0 and we use the fixed default r^+​(s,a)=r0​(s,a)\hat{r}^{+}(s,a)=r_{0}(s,a). Then

ε^r^+​(s,a)|N=0=r0​(s,a)−μr​(s,a),Var𝒟⁡(r^+​(s,a))|N=0=0.\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}(s,a)\big|_{N=0}=r_{0}(s,a)-\mu_{r}(s,a),\qquad\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal{D}}(\hat{r}^{+}(s,a))\big|_{N=0}=0. (54)

The baseline local objective is:

ϕ0:=α1​(μr​(s,a)−r0​(s,a))2.\phi_{0}:=\alpha_{1}\bigl(\mu_{r}(s,a)-r_{0}(s,a)\bigr)^{2}. (55)

For n≥1n\geq 1, N=nN=n and the local objective (Eq. 29) becomes:

ϕ⁡(n)=α1​n2​ε2+α3​n​σg2n2=α1​ε2+α3​σg2n,n≥1.\phi(n)=\frac{\alpha_{1}n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}n\sigma_{g}^{2}}{n^{2}}=\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}+\frac{\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}}{n},\qquad n\geq 1. (56)

Substituting nf=0n_{f}=0 into Eq. (42) gives 𝔞=−α3​σg2≤0\mathfrak{a}=-\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}\leq 0 and 𝔟=0\mathfrak{b}=0. The derivative ϕ′(n)=−α3σg2/n2≤0\phi^{\prime}(n)=-\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}/n^{2}\leq 0 shows that the local objective is nonincreasing for n≥1n\geq 1, with strict decrease exactly when α3​σg2>0\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}>0.

Proposition 4 (Properties When nf=0n_{f}=0 and πb​(a|s)>0\pi_{b}(a|s)>0).

For nf​(s,a)=0n_{f}(s,a)=0 and α1>0\alpha_{1}>0, the local objective has the following properties:

  1. 1.

    First Annotation Threshold The transition from n=0n=0 to n=1n=1 satisfies:

    δ​ϕ​(0→1):=ϕ⁡(1)−ϕ0=α1​[ε2−(μr−r0)2]+α3​σg2.\delta\phi(0\to 1):=\phi(1)-\phi_{0}=\alpha_{1}\bigl[\varepsilon^{2}-(\mu_{r}-r_{0})^{2}\bigr]+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}. (57)

    This is positive (i.e., the first annotation is locally harmful) if and only if

    ε2>(μr−r0)2−η​σg2.\varepsilon^{2}>(\mu_{r}-r_{0})^{2}-\eta\,\sigma_{g}^{2}. (58)

    Equality in (58) leaves the local objective unchanged, and reversing the strict inequality gives a strict decrease. For an exact default r0=μrr_{0}=\mu_{r}, the first annotation is locally harmful if and only if ε2+η​σg2>0\varepsilon^{2}+\eta\sigma_{g}^{2}>0. Conversely, if the default is poor ((μr−r0)2(\mu_{r}-r_{0})^{2} large), the first annotation can be beneficial even with high bias.

  2. 2.

    Nonincreasing objective for n≥1n\geq 1: The marginal benefit of the (n+1)(n+1)-th annotation is

    −δ​ϕ​(n)=α3​σg2n⁡(n+1)=O⁡(1n2).-\delta\phi(n)=\frac{\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}}{n(n+1)}=O\!\left(\frac{1}{n^{2}}\right). (59)

    The decrease is strict if α3​σg2>0\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}>0; otherwise, ϕ⁡(n)=α1​ε2\phi(n)=\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2} for every n≥1n\geq 1.

  3. 3.

    Bias is never diluted: The bias of the reward estimator is ε^r^+​(s,a)=ε\hat{\varepsilon}_{\hat{r}^{+}}(s,a)=\varepsilon for all n≥1n\geq 1, independent of the annotation count. Without factual data, there is no unbiased component to attenuate the annotation bias.

  4. 4.

    Irreducible floor: For n≥1n\geq 1, the local objective is bounded below by α1​ε2\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}, which cannot be reduced by increasing nn. A net improvement over the baseline (ϕ⁡(n)<ϕ0\phi(n)<\phi_{0} for some n≥1n\geq 1) requires:

    ε2<(μr−r0)2.\varepsilon^{2}<(\mu_{r}-r_{0})^{2}. (60)

    That is, the annotation bias must be strictly smaller in magnitude than the default model’s bias.

Proof.

(1) From Eqs. (56) and (55):

δ​ϕ​(0→1)\displaystyle\delta\phi(0\to 1) =ϕ⁡(1)−ϕ0\displaystyle=\phi(1)-\phi_{0}
=[α1​ε2+α3​σg2]−α1​(μr−r0)2\displaystyle=\bigl[\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}\bigr]-\alpha_{1}(\mu_{r}-r_{0})^{2}
=α1​[ε2−(μr−r0)2]+α3​σg2.\displaystyle=\alpha_{1}\bigl[\varepsilon^{2}-(\mu_{r}-r_{0})^{2}\bigr]+\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}.

Because α1>0\alpha_{1}>0, the condition δ​ϕ​(0→1)>0\delta\phi(0\to 1)>0 is equivalent to Eq. (58), with equality or the reversed strict inequality corresponding to zero or negative change, respectively. Substituting r0=μrr_{0}=\mu_{r} gives the exact-default statement.

(2) From Eq. (56), δϕ(n)=α3σg2(1/(n+1)−1/n)=−α3σg2/(n(n+1))≤0\delta\phi(n)=\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}(1/(n+1)-1/n)=-\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}/(n(n+1))\leq 0. The denominator is positive for n≥1n\geq 1, so the decrease is strict exactly when α3​σg2>0\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}>0, and its magnitude is at most α3​σg2/n2\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}/n^{2}. If α3​σg2=0\alpha_{3}\sigma_{g}^{2}=0, Eq. (56) gives the stated constant value.

(3) When nf=0n_{f}=0, B⁡(s,a)=n​εn=εB(s,a)=\frac{n\varepsilon}{n}=\varepsilon for all n≥1n\geq 1.

(4) Equation (56) gives ϕ⁡(n)≥α1​ε2\phi(n)\geq\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2} for every n≥1n\geq 1, with limn→∞ϕ⁡(n)=α1​ε2\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi(n)=\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}. If ϕ⁡(n)<ϕ0\phi(n)<\phi_{0} for a feasible n≥1n\geq 1, then α1​ε2<ϕ0=α1​(μr−r0)2\alpha_{1}\varepsilon^{2}<\phi_{0}=\alpha_{1}(\mu_{r}-r_{0})^{2}; dividing by α1>0\alpha_{1}>0 proves the necessary condition (60).

∎

B.8.2 πb​(a|s)=0\pi_{b}(a|s)=0 and nf​(s,a)=0n_{f}(s,a)=0

When πb​(a|s)=0\pi_{b}(a|s)=0, neither the fitting sample nor the evaluation sample contains observations of action aa at context ss. If also πe​(a|s)=0\pi_{e}(a|s)=0, the pair contributes nothing to the estimator or JJ, and the zero-weight convention gives α1​(s,a)=α3​(s,a)=0\alpha_{1}(s,a)=\alpha_{3}(s,a)=0. If πe​(a|s)>0\pi_{e}(a|s)>0, common support fails; at a context with d0​(s)>0d_{0}(s)>0, the importance-weighted correction cannot remove the reward-model error for that action. The unbiasedness guarantee and MSE decomposition in Theorem 1 therefore do not generally apply. This does not imply infinite variance: with one context, πb​(a1|s)=1\pi_{b}(a_{1}|s)=1, and πe​(a2|s)=1\pi_{e}(a_{2}|s)=1 for a1≠a2a_{1}\neq a_{2}, the estimator in (1) reduces to r^+​(s,a2)\hat{r}^{+}(s,a_{2}), which has finite variance under the stated moment assumptions but may be biased.

Appendix C Properties of the Objective Function

This appendix establishes the four structural properties of J⁡(𝐧)J(\mathbf{n}) claimed in Proposition 1 of the main text. Nonnegativity and boundedness hold for every valid instance; the remaining properties are established by counterexamples. We organize the proof into four parts, summarized below:

  1. (I)

    JJ is non-negative and bounded over ℱ\mathcal{F} (Proposition 5);

  2. (II)

    JJ is non-separable across actions within the same context (Proposition 6);

  3. (III)

    the continuous relaxation of JJ is neither convex nor concave (Proposition 7);

  4. (IV)

    JJ is neither submodular nor supermodular over annotation allocations (Corollary 3).

C.1 Decomposition and Notation

We use B⁡(s,a):=B⁡(s,a,𝐧)B(s,a):=B(s,a;\mathbf{n}) and W⁡(s,a):=W⁡(s,a,𝐧)W(s,a):=W(s,a;\mathbf{n}) as defined before (2), including the default-model case N⁡(s,a)=0N(s,a)=0. The objective decomposes as

J⁡(𝐧)=J1​(𝐧)−J2​(𝐧)+J3​(𝐧),J(\mathbf{n})\;=\;J_{1}(\mathbf{n})\;-\;J_{2}(\mathbf{n})\;+\;J_{3}(\mathbf{n}),

where the three components are:

J1​(𝐧)\displaystyle J_{1}(\mathbf{n}) =∑s∑aα1​(s,a)​B​(s,a)2,\displaystyle=\sum_{s}\sum_{a}\alpha_{1}(s,a)\,B(s,a)^{2},
J2​(𝐧)\displaystyle J_{2}(\mathbf{n}) =∑sd0​(s)​ℬs​(𝐧)2,\displaystyle=\sum_{s}d_{0}(s)\,\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})^{2},
J3​(𝐧)\displaystyle J_{3}(\mathbf{n}) =∑s∑aα3​(s,a)​W​(s,a).\displaystyle=\sum_{s}\sum_{a}\alpha_{3}(s,a)W(s,a).

For a fixed context-action pair (s,a)(s,a), we define:

N:=N⁡(s,a)=nf+∑knk,\displaystyle N\;:=\;N(s,a)=n_{f}+\textstyle\sum_{k}n_{k}, nf:=nf​(s,a),\displaystyle n_{f}\;:=\;n_{f}(s,a),
P:=∑k=1Knk​εgk​(s,a),\displaystyle P\;:=\;\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}\,\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(s,a), QD:=∑k=1Knk​Δgk​(s,a),\displaystyle Q_{D}\;:=\;\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}\,\Delta_{g_{k}}(s,a),
B⁡(s,a)=P/N(N>0),\displaystyle B(s,a)=P/N\quad(N>0), σ2:=σr2​(s,a),\displaystyle\sigma^{2}\;:=\;\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a),
α1​(s,a):=d0​(s)​πe​(a|s)2πb​(a|s),\displaystyle\alpha_{1}(s,a)\;:=\;d_{0}(s)\,\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}}{\pi_{b}(a|s)}, α3​(s,a)=(1−πb​(a|s))​α1​(s,a).\displaystyle\alpha_{3}(s,a)=\bigl(1-\pi_{b}(a|s)\bigr)\alpha_{1}(s,a).

For N>0N>0, W⁡(s,a)=σ2/N+QD/N2W(s,a)=\sigma^{2}/N+Q_{D}/N^{2}; for N=0N=0, we use B⁡(s,a)=r0​(s,a)−μr​(s,a)B(s,a)=r_{0}(s,a)-\mu_{r}(s,a) and W⁡(s,a)=0W(s,a)=0. The coefficients use the zero-weight convention α1=α3=0\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{3}=0 when πe​(a|s)=0\pi_{e}(a|s)=0. The context-level bias accumulation is

ℬs​(𝐧):=∑a∈𝒜πe​(a|s)​B​(s,a).\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})\;:=\;\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{e}(a|s)\,B(s,a).

We write Ek:=εgk​(s,a)E_{k}:=\varepsilon_{g_{k}}(s,a) and Dk:=Δgk​(s,a)D_{k}:=\Delta_{g_{k}}(s,a) when (s,a)(s,a) is clear from context. The shorthand njn_{j} denotes the annotation count nj​(s,a)n_{j}(s,a) from source jj for the pair under consideration.

We note the following elementary sign properties:

  • •

    α1​(s,a)≥0\alpha_{1}(s,a)\geq 0, with strict positivity exactly when d0​(s)>0d_{0}(s)>0 and πe​(a|s)>0\pi_{e}(a|s)>0 under common support;

  • •

    α3​(s,a)=α1​(s,a)−d0​(s)​πe​(a|s)2=(1−πb​(a|s))​α1​(s,a)≥0\alpha_{3}(s,a)=\alpha_{1}(s,a)-d_{0}(s)\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}=\bigl(1-\pi_{b}(a|s)\bigr)\alpha_{1}(s,a)\geq 0, with equality exactly when α1​(s,a)=0\alpha_{1}(s,a)=0 or πb​(a|s)=1\pi_{b}(a|s)=1.

C.2 First and Second-Order Derivatives

We compute all partial derivatives with respect to the annotation counts nk:=nk​(s,a)n_{k}:=n_{k}(s,a). Since J1J_{1} and J3J_{3} decompose over individual (s,a)(s,a) pairs while J2J_{2} decomposes over contexts, the analysis is organized accordingly. At N⁡(s,a)=0N(s,a)=0, finite annotation changes are evaluated using the default definitions rather than the rational derivative formulas below.

Lemma 5 (First-order partial derivatives).

For a fixed (s,a)(s,a) pair with N⁡(s,a)>0N(s,a)>0 and annotation source k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K}:

∂J1(s,a)∂nk\displaystyle\frac{\partial J_{1}^{(s,a)}}{\partial n_{k}} =2​α1​P​(Ek​N−P)N3,\displaystyle=\frac{2\alpha_{1}\,P\,(E_{k}N-P)}{N^{3}}, (61)
∂J2(s)∂nk​(s,a)\displaystyle\frac{\partial J_{2}^{(s)}}{\partial n_{k}(s,a)} =2​d0​(s)​ℬs​πe​(a|s)​Ek​N−PN2,\displaystyle=2\,d_{0}(s)\,\mathcal{B}_{s}\,\pi_{e}(a|s)\,\frac{E_{k}N-P}{N^{2}}, (62)
∂J3(s,a)∂nk\displaystyle\frac{\partial J_{3}^{(s,a)}}{\partial n_{k}} =α3N3​((Dk−σ2)​N−2​QD).\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{3}}{N^{3}}\Big((D_{k}-\sigma^{2})\,N-2\,Q_{D}\Big). (63)
Proof.

Eq. (61). Write J1(s,a)=α1​(P/N)2J_{1}^{(s,a)}=\alpha_{1}\,(P/N)^{2}. Noting ∂P∂nk=Ek\frac{\partial P}{\partial n_{k}}=E_{k} and ∂N∂nk=1\frac{\partial N}{\partial n_{k}}=1, the chain rule gives

∂∂nk​(PN)=Ek​N−PN2,\frac{\partial}{\partial n_{k}}\!\left(\frac{P}{N}\right)=\frac{E_{k}\,N-P}{N^{2}},

hence ∂J1(s,a)∂nk=2​α1⋅PN⋅Ek​N−PN2\frac{\partial J_{1}^{(s,a)}}{\partial n_{k}}=2\alpha_{1}\cdot\frac{P}{N}\cdot\frac{E_{k}N-P}{N^{2}}, yielding (61).

Eq. (62). Since ℬs=∑a′πe​(a′|s)​B​(s,a′)\mathcal{B}_{s}=\sum_{a^{\prime}}\pi_{e}(a^{\prime}|s)\,B(s,a^{\prime}) and only B⁡(s,a)B(s,a) depends on nk​(s,a)n_{k}(s,a):

∂ℬs∂nk​(s,a)=πe​(a|s)​Ek​N−PN2.\frac{\partial\mathcal{B}_{s}}{\partial n_{k}(s,a)}=\pi_{e}(a|s)\,\frac{E_{k}N-P}{N^{2}}.

Then ∂J2(s)∂nk​(s,a)=2​d0​(s)​ℬs⋅∂ℬs∂nk​(s,a)\frac{\partial J_{2}^{(s)}}{\partial n_{k}(s,a)}=2\,d_{0}(s)\,\mathcal{B}_{s}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathcal{B}_{s}}{\partial n_{k}(s,a)} gives (62).

Eq. (63). Writing J3(s,a)=α3​σ2​N−1+α3​QD​N−2J_{3}^{(s,a)}=\alpha_{3}\,\sigma^{2}N^{-1}+\alpha_{3}\,Q_{D}\,N^{-2} and differentiating:

∂J3(s,a)∂nk=α3​(−σ2N2+Dk​N−2​QDN3)=α3N3​((Dk−σ2)​N−2​QD).∎\frac{\partial J_{3}^{(s,a)}}{\partial n_{k}}=\alpha_{3}\!\left(-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{N^{2}}+\frac{D_{k}\,N-2\,Q_{D}}{N^{3}}\right)=\frac{\alpha_{3}}{N^{3}}\Big((D_{k}-\sigma^{2})N-2Q_{D}\Big).\qed
Lemma 6 (Hessian entries).

For a fixed context ss, the following second-order partial derivatives hold when every pair being differentiated has positive total count.

(i) J1(s,a)J_{1}^{(s,a)}: same pair, sources k,lk,l.
∂2J1(s,a)∂nk​∂nl=2​α1N4​(Ek​El​N2−2​(Ek+El)​P​N+3​P2).\frac{\partial^{2}J_{1}^{(s,a)}}{\partial n_{k}\,\partial n_{l}}=\frac{2\alpha_{1}}{N^{4}}\Big(E_{k}E_{l}\,N^{2}-2(E_{k}+E_{l})\,P\,N+3P^{2}\Big). (64)
(ii) J2(s)J_{2}^{(s)}: same action aa, sources k,lk,l.
∂2J2(s)∂nk​(s,a)​∂nl​(s,a)=2​d0​(s)​[πe​(a|s)2​(Ek​N−P)​(El​N−P)N4+ℬs​πe​(a|s)​(2​P−(Ek+El)​N)N3].\frac{\partial^{2}J_{2}^{(s)}}{\partial n_{k}(s,a)\,\partial n_{l}(s,a)}=2\,d_{0}(s)\!\left[\frac{\pi_{e}(a|s)^{2}\,(E_{k}N{-}P)(E_{l}N{-}P)}{N^{4}}+\frac{\mathcal{B}_{s}\,\pi_{e}(a|s)\,(2P{-}(E_{k}{+}E_{l})N)}{N^{3}}\right]\!. (65)
(iii) J2(s)J_{2}^{(s)}: different actions a≠a′a\neq a^{\prime}, sources k,lk,l.
∂2J2(s)∂nk​(s,a)​∂nl​(s,a′)=2​d0​(s)​πe​(a|s)​πe​(a′|s)​(Ek​Na−Pa)​(El​Na′−Pa′)Na2​Na′2,\frac{\partial^{2}J_{2}^{(s)}}{\partial n_{k}(s,a)\,\partial n_{l}(s,a^{\prime})}=\frac{2\,d_{0}(s)\,\pi_{e}(a|s)\,\pi_{e}(a^{\prime}|s)\,(E_{k}N_{a}-P_{a})(E_{l}N_{a^{\prime}}-P_{a^{\prime}})}{N_{a}^{2}\,N_{a^{\prime}}^{2}}, (66)

where Na:=N⁡(s,a)N_{a}:=N(s,a), Pa:=P⁡(s,a)P_{a}:=P(s,a), etc.

(iv) J3(s,a)J_{3}^{(s,a)}: same pair, sources k,lk,l.
∂2J3(s,a)∂nk​∂nl=2​α3N4​((σ2−Dk−Dl)​N+3​QD).\frac{\partial^{2}J_{3}^{(s,a)}}{\partial n_{k}\,\partial n_{l}}=\frac{2\alpha_{3}}{N^{4}}\Big((\sigma^{2}-D_{k}-D_{l})\,N+3\,Q_{D}\Big). (67)
Proof.

All four identities follow from applying the quotient rule to the first-order expressions in Lemma 5. We detail each computation below.

Part (i). Let u:=P/Nu:=P/N so that J1(s,a)=α1​u2J_{1}^{(s,a)}=\alpha_{1}u^{2}. From Lemma 5, ∂u∂nk=(Ek−u)/N\frac{\partial u}{\partial n_{k}}=(E_{k}-u)/N. Differentiating:

∂2(α1​u2)∂nk​∂nl\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}(\alpha_{1}u^{2})}{\partial n_{k}\,\partial n_{l}} =2​α1​(∂u∂nk​∂u∂nl+u​∂2u∂nk​∂nl).\displaystyle=2\alpha_{1}\!\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial n_{k}}\,\frac{\partial u}{\partial n_{l}}+u\,\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial n_{k}\,\partial n_{l}}\right).

We compute

∂2u∂nk​∂nl=∂∂nl​(Ek−uN)=−∂u∂nl​N−(Ek−u)N2=2​u−Ek−ElN2.\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial n_{k}\,\partial n_{l}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial n_{l}}\!\left(\frac{E_{k}-u}{N}\right)=\frac{-\frac{\partial u}{\partial n_{l}}\,N-(E_{k}-u)}{N^{2}}=\frac{2u-E_{k}-E_{l}}{N^{2}}.

Substituting and collecting terms with u=P/Nu=P/N:

∂2J1(s,a)∂nk​∂nl\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}J_{1}^{(s,a)}}{\partial n_{k}\,\partial n_{l}} =2​α1N2​[(Ek−u)​(El−u)+u⁡(2​u−Ek−El)]\displaystyle=\frac{2\alpha_{1}}{N^{2}}\!\left[(E_{k}-u)(E_{l}-u)+u(2u-E_{k}-E_{l})\right]
=2​α1N2​[Ek​El−2​(Ek+El)​u+3​u2],\displaystyle=\frac{2\alpha_{1}}{N^{2}}\!\left[E_{k}E_{l}-2(E_{k}+E_{l})u+3u^{2}\right],

which yields (64) after substituting u=P/Nu=P/N.

Part (ii). Differentiating (62) with respect to nl​(s,a)n_{l}(s,a):

∂2J2(s)∂nk​(s,a)​∂nl​(s,a)=2​d0​(s)​[∂ℬs∂nl⋅πe​(a|s)​Ek​N−PN2+ℬs⋅πe​(a|s)​∂∂nl​(Ek​N−PN2)].\frac{\partial^{2}J_{2}^{(s)}}{\partial n_{k}(s,a)\,\partial n_{l}(s,a)}=2\,d_{0}(s)\!\left[\frac{\partial\mathcal{B}_{s}}{\partial n_{l}}\!\cdot\!\pi_{e}(a|s)\frac{E_{k}N{-}P}{N^{2}}+\mathcal{B}_{s}\!\cdot\!\pi_{e}(a|s)\frac{\partial}{\partial n_{l}}\!\left(\frac{E_{k}N{-}P}{N^{2}}\right)\right].

Using ∂ℬs∂nl​(s,a)=πe​(a|s)​El​N−PN2\frac{\partial\mathcal{B}_{s}}{\partial n_{l}(s,a)}=\pi_{e}(a|s)\frac{E_{l}N-P}{N^{2}} from Lemma 5 and

∂∂nl​(Ek​N−PN2)=2​P−(Ek+El)​NN3,\frac{\partial}{\partial n_{l}}\!\left(\frac{E_{k}N-P}{N^{2}}\right)=\frac{2P-(E_{k}+E_{l})N}{N^{3}},

(computed via the quotient rule) yields (65).

Part (iii). For a≠a′a\neq a^{\prime}, since B⁡(s,a)B(s,a) depends only on {nk​(s,a)}k\{n_{k}(s,a)\}_{k} and B⁡(s,a′)B(s,a^{\prime}) depends only on {nk​(s,a′)}k\{n_{k}(s,a^{\prime})\}_{k}, the term ℬs⋅∂∂nl​(s,a′)​(⋯)\mathcal{B}_{s}\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial n_{l}(s,a^{\prime})}(\cdots) does not contribute a cross-action second derivative from the same factor. Only the product of first derivatives remains:

∂2J2(s)∂nk​(s,a)​∂nl​(s,a′)=2​d0​(s)​∂ℬs∂nk​(s,a)​∂ℬs∂nl​(s,a′),\frac{\partial^{2}J_{2}^{(s)}}{\partial n_{k}(s,a)\,\partial n_{l}(s,a^{\prime})}=2\,d_{0}(s)\,\frac{\partial\mathcal{B}_{s}}{\partial n_{k}(s,a)}\,\frac{\partial\mathcal{B}_{s}}{\partial n_{l}(s,a^{\prime})},

giving (66).

Part (iv). Let Rk:=(Dk−σ2)​N−2​QDR_{k}:=(D_{k}-\sigma^{2})N-2Q_{D} so that ∂J3(s,a)∂nk=α3​Rk/N3\frac{\partial J_{3}^{(s,a)}}{\partial n_{k}}=\alpha_{3}R_{k}/N^{3}. Then ∂Rk∂nl=(Dk−σ2)−2​Dl\frac{\partial R_{k}}{\partial n_{l}}=(D_{k}-\sigma^{2})-2D_{l}, and the quotient rule gives:

(Dk−σ2−2​Dl)​N−3​(Dk−σ2)​N+6​QD=2​(σ2−Dk−Dl)​N+6​QD.∎(D_{k}-\sigma^{2}-2D_{l})N-3(D_{k}-\sigma^{2})N+6Q_{D}=2(\sigma^{2}-D_{k}-D_{l})N+6Q_{D}.\qed
Hessian matrices in compact form.

For a fixed (s,a)(s,a), define the vectors 𝐞=(E1,…,EK)⊤\mathbf{e}=(E_{1},\ldots,E_{K})^{\top}, 𝐝=(D1,…,DK)⊤\mathbf{d}=(D_{1},\ldots,D_{K})^{\top}, and 𝟏=(1,…,1)⊤∈ℝK\mathbf{1}=(1,\ldots,1)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}. The Hessian matrices 𝐇1,𝐇3∈ℝK×K\mathbf{H}_{1},\mathbf{H}_{3}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K} with respect to (n1,…,nK)(n_{1},\ldots,n_{K}) for the given (s,a)(s,a) pair are:

𝐇1\displaystyle\mathbf{H}_{1} =2​α1N4​(N2​𝐞𝐞⊤−2​N​P​(𝐞𝟏⊤+𝟏​𝐞⊤)+3​P2​ 11⊤),\displaystyle=\frac{2\alpha_{1}}{N^{4}}\!\left(N^{2}\,\mathbf{e}\mathbf{e}^{\top}-2NP\,(\mathbf{e}\mathbf{1}^{\top}+\mathbf{1}\mathbf{e}^{\top})+3P^{2}\,\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\right),
𝐇3\displaystyle\mathbf{H}_{3} =2​α3N4​((σ2​N+3​QD)​ 11⊤−N⁡(𝐝𝟏⊤+𝟏​𝐝⊤)).\displaystyle=\frac{2\alpha_{3}}{N^{4}}\!\left((\sigma^{2}N+3Q_{D})\,\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}-N\,(\mathbf{d}\mathbf{1}^{\top}+\mathbf{1}\mathbf{d}^{\top})\right).

Both are sums of rank-one and rank-two matrices; their spectral properties are parameter-dependent and analyzed in §C.3.

C.3 Structural Properties

We now prove the structural claims in Proposition 1.

Proposition 5 (Non-negativity and boundedness).

For every feasible allocation 𝐧∈ℱ\mathbf{n}\in\mathcal{F},

0≤J⁡(𝐧)≤Jmax<∞.0\;\leq\;J(\mathbf{n})\;\leq\;J_{\max}<\infty.

(∑awa​xa)2⏟=ℬs2=(∑aca⋅wa​xaca)2≤(∑aca)​(∑awa2ca​xa2)=∑awa2ca​xa2,\underbrace{\left(\sum_{a}w_{a}\,x_{a}\right)^{2}}_{\textstyle=\mathcal{B}_{s}^{2}}=\left(\sum_{a}\sqrt{c_{a}}\cdot\frac{w_{a}\,x_{a}}{\sqrt{c_{a}}}\right)^{2}\leq\left(\sum_{a}c_{a}\right)\!\left(\sum_{a}\frac{w_{a}^{2}}{c_{a}}\,x_{a}^{2}\right)=\sum_{a}\frac{w_{a}^{2}}{c_{a}}\,x_{a}^{2},

where we used ∑aca=∑aπb​(a|s)=1\sum_{a}c_{a}=\sum_{a}\pi_{b}(a|s)=1. Multiplying both sides by d0​(s)d_{0}(s) and summing over ss yields J2​(𝐧)≤J1​(𝐧)J_{2}(\mathbf{n})\leq J_{1}(\mathbf{n}), hence J1−J2≥0J_{1}-J_{2}\geq 0.

For J3J_{3}, pairs with N⁡(s,a)=0N(s,a)=0 have W⁡(s,a)=0W(s,a)=0 and contribute zero. For a pair with N⁡(s,a)>0N(s,a)>0, combining the two terms in W⁡(s,a)W(s,a) gives

Proposition 6 (Non-separability across actions).

There exist valid instances with a single context ss and |𝒜|≥2|\mathcal{A}|\geq 2 for which no functions {fa}a∈𝒜\{f_{a}\}_{a\in\mathcal{A}} satisfy

Proof.

We first identify the cross-action coupling in the continuous relaxation, then verify non-separability on feasible integer allocations.

Since J1J_{1} and J3J_{3} decompose over individual (s,a)(s,a) pairs, they contribute zero to the cross-action derivative. The only contribution comes from −J2-J_{2}. By Lemma 6(iii):

which is non-zero whenever d0​(s)>0d_{0}(s)>0, πe​(a|s),πe​(a′|s)>0\pi_{e}(a|s),\pi_{e}(a^{\prime}|s)>0, and Ek,El≠0E_{k},E_{l}\neq 0.

For integer allocations, we choose one context, two actions, one source, and πb​(ai|s)=πe​(ai|s)=1/2\pi_{b}(a_{i}|s)=\pi_{e}(a_{i}|s)=1/2 for i=1,2i=1,2. Writing J⁡(x,y)J(x,y) for the objective at counts xx and yy on the two actions, substitution into (2) gives

J⁡(0,0)=12,J⁡(1,0)=J⁡(0,1)=716,J⁡(1,1)=14.J(0,0)=\frac{1}{2},\qquad J(1,0)=J(0,1)=\frac{7}{16},\qquad J(1,1)=\frac{1}{4}.

Proposition 7 (Non-convexity and non-concavity).

There exist valid instances for which the continuous relaxation of J⁡(𝐧)J(\mathbf{n}) is neither convex nor concave over feasible allocations.

Proof.

We show non-convexity and non-concavity by exhibiting a feasible direction along which a diagonal entry of the Hessian of the continuous relaxation takes opposite signs at two configurations.

We construct an instance with one context ss, two actions 𝒜={a1,a2}\mathcal{A}=\{a_{1},a_{2}\}, a single annotation source (K=1K=1), and πb​(a1|s)=πb​(a2|s)=1/2\pi_{b}(a_{1}|s)=\pi_{b}(a_{2}|s)=1/2. Set πe​(a1|s)=1\pi_{e}(a_{1}|s)=1 and πe​(a2|s)=0\pi_{e}(a_{2}|s)=0, and fix n1​(s,a2)=0n_{1}(s,a_{2})=0, so the only decision variable is n:=n1​(s,a1)n:=n_{1}(s,a_{1}). Write

E:=εg1​(s,a1),D:=Δg1​(s,a1),σ2:=σr2​(s,a1),nf:=nf​(s,a1),N:=nf+n.E:=\varepsilon_{g_{1}}(s,a_{1}),\quad D:=\Delta_{g_{1}}(s,a_{1}),\quad\sigma^{2}:=\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a_{1}),\quad n_{f}:=n_{f}(s,a_{1}),\quad N:=n_{f}+n.

We choose a positive integer nfn_{f}, set nf​(s,a2)=2​nfn_{f}(s,a_{2})=2n_{f}, c1=1c_{1}=1, and κ=2​nf\kappa=2n_{f}; then Ns=3​nfN_{s}=3n_{f} and the feasible interval along this direction is 0≤n≤2​nf0\leq n\leq 2n_{f}. Under this configuration, only (s,a1)(s,a_{1}) contributes to the bias-related terms, and ℬs​(𝐧)=πe​(a1|s)​B​(s,a1)=B⁡(s,a1)\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})=\pi_{e}(a_{1}|s)\,B(s,a_{1})=B(s,a_{1}). Using the identity α1​(s,a1)−d0​(s)​πe​(a1|s)2=α3​(s,a1)\alpha_{1}(s,a_{1})-d_{0}(s)\pi_{e}(a_{1}|s)^{2}=\alpha_{3}(s,a_{1}) (Eq. (53)), the contribution of (s,a1)(s,a_{1}) to J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} collapses into α3​(s,a1)​B​(s,a1)2\alpha_{3}(s,a_{1})\,B(s,a_{1})^{2}. Thus, along this feasible direction,

J⁡(n)=α3​[n2​E2N2+σ2N+n​DN2],α3:=α3​(s,a1)>0.J(n)=\alpha_{3}\!\left[\frac{n^{2}E^{2}}{N^{2}}+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{N}+\frac{nD}{N^{2}}\right],\qquad\alpha_{3}:=\alpha_{3}(s,a_{1})>0.

Specializing the Hessian formulas of Lemma 6(i) and (iv) to K=1K=1 (so that the mixed partial reduces to the second derivative), the diagonal entry of the Hessian is

J′′​(n)=2​α3N4​[E2​nf​(nf−2​n)+(σ2−2​D)​N+3​n​D].J^{\prime\prime}(n)=\frac{2\alpha_{3}}{N^{4}}\!\left[E^{2}\,n_{f}(n_{f}-2n)+(\sigma^{2}-2D)\,N+3nD\right]. (69)

Non-concavity. Evaluating (69) at n=0n=0 (so N=nfN=n_{f}):

J′′​(0)=2​α3nf4​[E2​nf2+(σ2−2​D)​nf]=2​α3​(E2​nf+σ2−2​D)nf3.J^{\prime\prime}(0)=\frac{2\alpha_{3}}{n_{f}^{4}}\!\left[E^{2}n_{f}^{2}+(\sigma^{2}-2D)n_{f}\right]=\frac{2\alpha_{3}\bigl(E^{2}n_{f}+\sigma^{2}-2D\bigr)}{n_{f}^{3}}.

For α3>0\alpha_{3}>0 and parameters with E2​nf+σ2−2​D>0E^{2}n_{f}+\sigma^{2}-2D>0 (e.g. E≠0E\neq 0 and 0≤D≤σ2/20\leq D\leq\sigma^{2}/2), J′′​(0)>0J^{\prime\prime}(0)>0. By continuity, J′′​(n)>0J^{\prime\prime}(n)>0 at interior points of the feasible interval sufficiently close to zero, so JJ is not concave.

Non-convexity. At n=nfn=n_{f} (so N=2​nfN=2n_{f}):

J′′​(nf)=2​α3(2​nf)4​[−E2​nf2+2​(σ2−2​D)​nf+3​nf​D]=α3​(−E2​nf+2​σ2−D)8​nf3.J^{\prime\prime}(n_{f})=\frac{2\alpha_{3}}{(2n_{f})^{4}}\!\left[-E^{2}n_{f}^{2}+2(\sigma^{2}-2D)n_{f}+3n_{f}D\right]=\frac{\alpha_{3}\bigl(-E^{2}n_{f}+2\sigma^{2}-D\bigr)}{8\,n_{f}^{3}}.
