Corollary 3 (Neither submodular nor supermodular).

There exist valid instances for which J⁡(𝐧)J(\mathbf{n}), viewed as a function on the integer lattice ℤ+|𝒮|​|𝒜|​K\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{A}|K}, is neither submodular nor supermodular, with both properties violated by feasible allocations.

Proof.

We test the defining lattice inequality on feasible integer allocations. Submodularity requires J⁡(𝐱)+J⁡(𝐲)≥J⁡(𝐱∧𝐲)+J⁡(𝐱∨𝐲)J(\mathbf{x})+J(\mathbf{y})\geq J(\mathbf{x}\wedge\mathbf{y})+J(\mathbf{x}\vee\mathbf{y}), where ∧\wedge and ∨\vee denote coordinate-wise minimum and maximum; supermodularity requires the reverse inequality. For distinct coordinates i,ji,j with unit vectors 𝐞i,𝐞j\mathbf{e}_{i},\mathbf{e}_{j}, we define the mixed finite difference

δi​j​J​(𝐧):=J⁡(𝐧+𝐞i+𝐞j)−J⁡(𝐧+𝐞i)−J⁡(𝐧+𝐞j)+J⁡(𝐧).\delta_{ij}J(\mathbf{n}):=J(\mathbf{n}+\mathbf{e}_{i}+\mathbf{e}_{j})-J(\mathbf{n}+\mathbf{e}_{i})-J(\mathbf{n}+\mathbf{e}_{j})+J(\mathbf{n}).

Taking 𝐱=𝐧+𝐞i\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{n}+\mathbf{e}_{i} and 𝐲=𝐧+𝐞j\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{n}+\mathbf{e}_{j} shows that submodularity requires δi​j​J​(𝐧)≤0\delta_{ij}J(\mathbf{n})\leq 0, whereas supermodularity requires δi​j​J​(𝐧)≥0\delta_{ij}J(\mathbf{n})\geq 0.

We construct one instance violating both requirements, with one context ss, three actions a1,a2,a3a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}, and one source. For each action, we set πb​(ai|s)=πe​(ai|s)=1/3\pi_{b}(a_{i}|s)=\pi_{e}(a_{i}|s)=1/3, nf​(s,ai)=1n_{f}(s,a_{i})=1, σr2​(s,ai)=1\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a_{i})=1, and Δg1​(s,ai)=0\Delta_{g_{1}}(s,a_{i})=0. We write εi:=εg1​(s,ai)\varepsilon_{i}:=\varepsilon_{g_{1}}(s,a_{i}) and choose (ε1,ε2,ε3)=(1,1,−1)(\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2},\varepsilon_{3})=(1,1,-1). These moments can be realized by independent rewards taking values 11 and 33 with equal probability, with each annotation distributed as an independent reward draw plus the corresponding bias. We set c1=1c_{1}=1 and κ=2\kappa=2, giving Ns=3N_{s}=3 and per-action capacities Ns−nf​(s,ai)=2N_{s}-n_{f}(s,a_{i})=2. Thus 𝟎\mathbf{0}, 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i}, 𝐞j\mathbf{e}_{j}, and 𝐞i+𝐞j\mathbf{e}_{i}+\mathbf{e}_{j} are feasible for every i≠ji\neq j, where 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i} now denotes one annotation for action aia_{i}.

The terms J1J_{1} and J3J_{3} are sums of per-action functions, so their mixed finite differences vanish. At the zero allocation, all reward-model biases are zero; adding one annotation for action aia_{i} gives B⁡(s,ai)=εi/2B(s,a_{i})=\varepsilon_{i}/2. Consequently, ℬs​(𝟎)=0\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{0})=0, ℬs​(𝐞i)=εi/6\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{e}_{i})=\varepsilon_{i}/6, and ℬs​(𝐞i+𝐞j)=(εi+εj)/6\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{e}_{i}+\mathbf{e}_{j})=(\varepsilon_{i}+\varepsilon_{j})/6. Only −J2=−ℬs2-J_{2}=-\mathcal{B}_{s}^{2} contributes to the mixed difference, yielding

δi​j​J​(𝟎)=−(εi+εj)2−εi2−εj236=−εi​εj18.\delta_{ij}J(\mathbf{0})=-\frac{(\varepsilon_{i}+\varepsilon_{j})^{2}-\varepsilon_{i}^{2}-\varepsilon_{j}^{2}}{36}=-\frac{\varepsilon_{i}\varepsilon_{j}}{18}.

Hence δ12J(𝟎)=−1/18<0\delta_{12}J(\mathbf{0})=-1/18<0 violates supermodularity, while δ13​J​(𝟎)=1/18>0\delta_{13}J(\mathbf{0})=1/18>0 violates submodularity on the same instance. The same violations persist with additional sources by setting their annotation counts to zero. ∎

Appendix D Analysis of the Majorization-Minimization Algorithm

This appendix provides the theoretical analysis of the proposed MM framework. Throughout this section, we use the notation established in §C.1. In particular, ℬs​(𝐧):=∑a∈𝒜πe​(a|s)​B​(s,a)\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}):=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{e}(a|s)B(s,a) denotes the context-level bias accumulation, with BB and WW defined in (2) and its preceding text, including the default-model case N⁡(s,a)=0N(s,a)=0. We write ℱ\mathcal{F} for the full feasible set defined by all constraints in (3), and ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} for the feasible set with the budget constraint removed.

D.1 Pseudocode of the Algorithms

Algorithm 1 retains the best feasible allocation found at each majorization-minimization (MM) iteration, while Algorithm 2 generates candidates by local source search and dynamic programming (DP). Both algorithms use factual fitting counts, reward moments, source profiles, policy probabilities, default rewards, and costs from the allocation problem; these fixed inputs are suppressed in subroutine calls. The MM coefficients are ω1​(s,a)=α1​(s,a)\omega_{1}(s,a)=\alpha_{1}(s,a), ω3​(s,a)=α3​(s,a)\omega_{3}(s,a)=\alpha_{3}(s,a), and ω2(t)​(s,a)=−2​d0​(s)​ℬs​(𝐧(t))​πe​(a|s)\omega_{2}^{(t)}(s,a)=-2d_{0}(s)\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})\pi_{e}(a|s). The local search and DP tables use the complete penalized cost ψs,a(t)​(𝐳,λ):=J~s,a(t)​(𝐳)+λ​∑kck​zk\psi_{s,a}^{(t)}(\mathbf{z};\lambda):=\tilde{J}_{s,a}^{(t)}(\mathbf{z})+\lambda\sum_{k}c_{k}z_{k}, where J~s,a(t)\tilde{J}_{s,a}^{(t)} is the summand defined in §6.2. For each total count mm, the subproblem solver records the largest remaining positive swap gain δs,a​(m,λ)\delta_{s,a}(m,\lambda), with zero assigned when no improving swap exists. These residuals certify the approximation error even when the swap cap is reached (Proposition 9). All ties in source selection, swaps, DP, and candidate ordering use a fixed index order, and the outer update retains the current allocation unless the surrogate strictly improves.

D.2 Surrogate Construction and Majorization Property

The MM framework replaces the non-convex objective J⁡(𝐧)J(\mathbf{n}) with a locally tight upper bound. To remove the cross-action coupling, we majorize −J2(𝐧)=−∑sd0(s)ℬs(𝐧)2-J_{2}(\mathbf{n})=-\sum_{s}d_{0}(s)\,\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})^{2} while retaining J1J_{1} and J3J_{3}. We apply the tangent majorant of the concave scalar function h⁡(x)=−x2h(x)=-x^{2} at x=ℬs​(𝐧(t))x=\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}), giving an expression affine in ℬs​(𝐧)\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}).

Lemma 7 (Valid Majorization).

For any fixed feasible allocation 𝐧(t)\mathbf{n}^{(t)}, the full surrogate J~full​(𝐧,𝐧(t))\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)}) defined in Proposition 2 of §6.1 satisfies:

  1. (i)

    (Upper bound) J~full​(𝐧,𝐧(t))≥J⁡(𝐧)\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)})\geq J(\mathbf{n}) for all 𝐧∈ℱ\mathbf{n}\in\mathcal{F}.

  2. (ii)

    (Tangency) J~full​(𝐧(t),𝐧(t))=J⁡(𝐧(t))\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})=J(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}).

Moreover, the majorization gap admits the closed-form expression:

J~full​(𝐧,𝐧(t))−J⁡(𝐧)=∑s∈𝒮d0​(s)​(ℬs​(𝐧)−ℬs​(𝐧(t)))2.\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)})-J(\mathbf{n})=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\bigl(\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})-\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})\bigr)^{2}. (70)
Proof.

We fix 𝐧(t)∈ℱ\mathbf{n}^{(t)}\in\mathcal{F} and any 𝐧∈ℱ\mathbf{n}\in\mathcal{F}. Because h⁡(x)=−x2h(x)=-x^{2} is concave, its tangent at any x0∈ℝx_{0}\in\mathbb{R} gives a global upper bound:

−x2≤−x02−2​x0​(x−x0)=x02−2​x0​x,∀x∈ℝ,-x^{2}\;\leq\;-x_{0}^{2}-2x_{0}(x-x_{0})\;=\;x_{0}^{2}-2x_{0}\,x,\qquad\forall\,x\in\mathbb{R},

with equality if and only if x=x0x=x_{0}. Substituting x=ℬs​(𝐧)x=\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}) and x0=ℬs​(𝐧(t))x_{0}=\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}), multiplying by the nonnegative weights d0​(s)d_{0}(s), and summing over contexts gives

−∑sd0(s)ℬs(𝐧)2≤∑sd0(s)[ℬs(𝐧(t))2−2ℬs(𝐧(t))ℬs(𝐧)].-\sum_{s}d_{0}(s)\,\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})^{2}\;\leq\;\sum_{s}d_{0}(s)\bigl[\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})^{2}-2\,\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})\,\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})\bigr].

The full surrogate (including the constant term) is:

J~full​(𝐧,𝐧(t))=J1​(𝐧)+∑sd0​(s)​[ℬs​(𝐧(t))2−2​ℬs​(𝐧(t))​ℬs​(𝐧)]+J3​(𝐧).\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)})=J_{1}(\mathbf{n})+\sum_{s}d_{0}(s)\bigl[\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})^{2}-2\,\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})\,\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})\bigr]+J_{3}(\mathbf{n}). (71)

Property (i) follows from −J2​(𝐧)≤J~full​(𝐧,𝐧(t))−J1​(𝐧)−J3​(𝐧)-J_{2}(\mathbf{n})\leq\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)})-J_{1}(\mathbf{n})-J_{3}(\mathbf{n}). At 𝐧=𝐧(t)\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{n}^{(t)}, the summed linearized term in (71) equals

∑sd0(s)[(ℬs(t))2−2(ℬs(t))2]=−∑sd0(s)(ℬs(t))2=−J2(𝐧(t)).\sum_{s}d_{0}(s)\bigl[(\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(t)})^{2}-2(\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(t)})^{2}\bigr]=-\sum_{s}d_{0}(s)(\mathcal{B}_{s}^{(t)})^{2}=-J_{2}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}).

Substitution into (71) gives J~full​(𝐧(t),𝐧(t))=J1​(𝐧(t))−J2​(𝐧(t))+J3​(𝐧(t))=J⁡(𝐧(t))\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})=J_{1}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})-J_{2}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})+J_{3}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})=J(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}), proving property (ii).

For the gap formula, we compute:

J~full​(𝐧,𝐧(t))−J⁡(𝐧)\displaystyle\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)})-J(\mathbf{n})
=∑sd0​(s)​[ℬs​(𝐧(t))2−2​ℬs​(𝐧(t))​ℬs​(𝐧)+ℬs​(𝐧)2]\displaystyle=\sum_{s}d_{0}(s)\bigl[\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})^{2}-2\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})+\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})^{2}\bigr]
=∑sd0​(s)​(ℬs​(𝐧)−ℬs​(𝐧(t)))2.\displaystyle=\sum_{s}d_{0}(s)\bigl(\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n})-\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})\bigr)^{2}.

The optimization surrogate in (8) satisfies

J~​(𝐧,𝐧(t))=J~full​(𝐧,𝐧(t))−J2​(𝐧(t)).\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})=\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})-J_{2}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}).

Because J2​(𝐧(t))J_{2}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}) is independent of 𝐧\mathbf{n}, both surrogates have the same minimizers and give the same comparisons between allocations at fixed tt. At the current allocation, however, J~​(𝐧(t),𝐧(t))=J⁡(𝐧(t))−J2​(𝐧(t))\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})=J(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})-J_{2}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}). ∎

Proposition 8 (Monotone Descent under Surrogate-Improving Updates).

Suppose at every iteration t≥0t\geq 0 the update 𝐧(t+1)∈ℱ\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)}\in\mathcal{F} satisfies the surrogate-improvement condition

J~​(𝐧(t+1),𝐧(t))≤J~​(𝐧(t),𝐧(t)).\tilde{J}\!\bigl(\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)}\bigr)\;\leq\;\tilde{J}\!\bigl(\mathbf{n}^{(t)};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)}\bigr). (72)

Then the original objective is monotonically non-increasing,

J⁡(𝐧(t+1))≤J⁡(𝐧(t)),∀t≥0,J\!\bigl(\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)}\bigr)\;\leq\;J\!\bigl(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}\bigr),\qquad\forall\,t\geq 0,

and the sequence {J⁡(𝐧(t))}\{J(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})\} converges. The fallback rule 𝐧(t+1)←𝐧(t)\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\mathbf{n}^{(t)} used in Algorithm 1 ensures (72) regardless of how accurately the inner Lagrangian subproblem is solved; in particular, exact surrogate minimization is not required for descent of JJ.

Proof.

At fixed tt, adding J2​(𝐧(t))J_{2}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}) to both sides of (72) gives the same improvement inequality for J~full\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}. Combining this inequality with the upper bound and tangency in Lemma 7 yields

J⁡(𝐧(t+1))\displaystyle J(\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)}) ≤J~full​(𝐧(t+1),𝐧(t))\displaystyle\leq\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})
≤J~full​(𝐧(t),𝐧(t))\displaystyle\leq\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})
=J⁡(𝐧(t)).\displaystyle=J(\mathbf{n}^{(t)}).

The fallback update satisfies (72) with equality. Proposition 5 gives J≥0J\geq 0, so the non-increasing objective sequence converges. ∎

Remark 2 (Reconciliation with Theorem 6).

Proposition 8 only certifies monotonic descent of JJ along the iterates produced by Algorithm 1. It is independent of the suboptimality of 𝐧(t+1)\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)} relative to the exact constrained minimizer 𝐧^(t+1)=arg⁡minℱ​J~​(⋅,𝐧(t))\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{(t+1)}=\arg\min_{\mathcal{F}}\tilde{J}(\cdot;\mathbf{n}^{(t)}). Theorem 6 subsequently bounds the gap to the global minimizer 𝐧∗\mathbf{n}^{*} of JJ, and that bound naturally incorporates Inner-loop suboptimality (Proposition 10). The two results therefore play complementary roles: Proposition 8 guarantees algorithmic stability, while Theorem 6 quantifies how close each iterate may be to a global optimum.

D.3 Local Source Search and Exact Count Aggregation

At a fixed multiplier λ\lambda, separability allows us to search source mixtures independently and then aggregate their costs across actions. We bound the local-search error before propagating it through the exact DP aggregation.

Lemma 8 (Separability of the Surrogate).

The surrogate objective J~​(𝐧,𝐧(t))\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)}) decomposes as:

J~​(𝐧,𝐧(t))=∑s∈𝒮∑a∈𝒜ϕs,a(t)​({nk​(s,a)}k=1K).\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)})=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\phi_{s,a}^{(t)}\!\bigl(\{n_{k}(s,a)\}_{k=1}^{K}\bigr).

Here ϕs,a(t)=J~s,a(t)\phi_{s,a}^{(t)}=\tilde{J}_{s,a}^{(t)} is the local summand from §6.2 and depends only on the annotation counts for (s,a)(s,a).

The terms J1J_{1} and J3J_{3} are already sums over individual (s,a)(s,a) pairs. The linearized −J2-J_{2} contribution to the surrogate is:

−2∑sd0(s)ℬs(𝐧(t))∑aπe(a|s)B(s,a)=∑s∑aω2(t)(s,a)B(s,a),-2\sum_{s}d_{0}(s)\,\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})\!\sum_{a}\pi_{e}(a|s)\,B(s,a)=\sum_{s}\sum_{a}\omega_{2}^{(t)}(s,a)\,B(s,a),

where ω2(t)​(s,a)=−2​d0​(s)​ℬs​(𝐧(t))​πe​(a|s)\omega_{2}^{(t)}(s,a)=-2\,d_{0}(s)\,\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})\,\pi_{e}(a|s) is a constant with respect to 𝐧\mathbf{n}. Because each B⁡(s,a)B(s,a) depends only on {nk​(s,a)}k\{n_{k}(s,a)\}_{k}, the optimization surrogate J~\tilde{J} is separable. ∎

Lemma 9 (Convexity of the Local Cost for Fixed Total Count).

Fix an MM iteration tt, a pair (s,a)(s,a), a multiplier λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, and a total count mm with N0:=nf​(s,a)+m>0N_{0}:=n_{f}(s,a)+m>0. Holding N0N_{0} constant, the complete local cost is

ψs,a(t)​(𝐧K,λ)\displaystyle\psi_{s,a}^{(t)}(\mathbf{n}_{K};\lambda) =ω1N02​(∑knk​Ek)2+ω2(t)N0​∑knk​Ek\displaystyle=\frac{\omega_{1}}{N_{0}^{2}}\left(\sum_{k}n_{k}E_{k}\right)^{2}+\frac{\omega_{2}^{(t)}}{N_{0}}\sum_{k}n_{k}E_{k} (73)

The Hessian of ψ\psi with respect to 𝐧K\mathbf{n}_{K} is

𝐇ψ=2​ω1N02​𝐞​𝐞⊤,𝐞=(E1,…,EK)⊤.\mathbf{H}_{\psi}=\frac{2\omega_{1}}{N_{0}^{2}}\,\mathbf{e}\,\mathbf{e}^{\top},\qquad\mathbf{e}=(E_{1},\ldots,E_{K})^{\top}.

D.4 Lagrangian Relaxation Analysis

The global budget constraint ∑s,a,kck​nk​(s,a)≤κ\sum_{s,a,k}c_{k}\,n_{k}(s,a)\leq\kappa couples the subproblems across contexts. We relax it via a Lagrange multiplier λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, yielding the dual function:

q⁡(λ)=min𝐧∈ℱ0⁡{J~​(𝐧,𝐧(t))+λ⁡(∑s,a,kck​nk​(s,a)−κ)}.q(\lambda)=\min_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathcal{F}_{0}}\Bigl\{\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)})+\lambda\bigl(\textstyle\sum_{s,a,k}c_{k}\,n_{k}(s,a)-\kappa\bigr)\Bigr\}.

By Lemma 8, the Lagrangian problem decomposes over contexts. Algorithm 2 solves the count aggregation exactly for its supplied H♯H^{\sharp} tables; the local approximation errors determine its gap to the exact Lagrangian minimum.

The multiplier search always produces a feasible candidate in exact arithmetic. Indeed, ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} is finite, 𝟎\mathbf{0} is represented in every set of DP tables, and cmin:=mink⁡ck>0c_{\min}:=\min_{k}c_{k}>0. For fixed tt, every nonzero allocation has cost at least cminc_{\min}, so any

λ>J~​(𝟎,𝐧(t))−min𝐧∈ℱ0⁡J~​(𝐧,𝐧(t))cmin\lambda>\frac{\tilde{J}(\mathbf{0};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})-\min_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathcal{F}_{0}}\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})}{c_{\min}}

makes the zero allocation strictly better than every nonzero allocation in the penalized objective. Thus doubling eventually returns 𝟎\mathbf{0}, or terminates earlier at another budget-feasible candidate. Subsequent bisection is a finite candidate search, without a monotonicity guarantee for the costs returned by approximate local solves.

Proposition 10 (Inner-loop suboptimality).

Fix tt and let 𝐧^(t+1)∈arg⁡min𝐧∈ℱ​J~​(𝐧,𝐧(t))\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{(t+1)}\in\arg\min_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathcal{F}}\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n};\mathbf{n}^{(t)}). Choose any recorded feasible trial (λ(t),𝐧cand(t),𝛅(t))∈𝒬t(\lambda^{(t)},\mathbf{n}_{\mathrm{cand}}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(t)})\in\mathcal{Q}_{t} from Algorithm 1. EGreedy(t):=∑s,amax0≤m≤Ms,a⁡{ηs,a​(m)+m​δs,a​(m,λ(t))},E_{\mathrm{Greedy}}^{(t)}:=\sum_{s,a}\max_{0\leq m\leq M_{s,a}}\left\{\eta_{s,a}(m)+m\,\delta_{s,a}(m,\lambda^{(t)})\right\},

0≤ΔLag(t)\displaystyle 0\leq\Delta_{\mathrm{Lag}}^{(t)} :=J~​(𝐧(t+1),𝐧(t))−J~​(𝐧^(t+1),𝐧(t))\displaystyle:=\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})-\tilde{J}(\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{(t+1)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)}) (76)

Feasibility of 𝐧(t+1)\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)} and optimality of 𝐧^(t+1)\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{(t+1)} give ΔLag(t)≥0\Delta_{\mathrm{Lag}}^{(t)}\geq 0. For the upper bound, fix the selected trial multiplier λ=λ(t)\lambda=\lambda^{(t)} and write L⁡(𝐧,λ):=J~​(𝐧,𝐧(t))+λ​C​(𝐧)L(\mathbf{n};\lambda):=\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})+\lambda C(\mathbf{n}).

Minimizing over these choices proves the interpretation inductively and supplies valid backtracking counts. Selecting the best w≤Nsw\leq N_{s} enforces the context capacity inequality. Assembling the independent context solutions therefore minimizes the sum of stored costs over ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0}.

Let 𝐧~λ∈arg⁡min𝐧∈ℱ0⁡L⁡(𝐧,λ)\tilde{\mathbf{n}}_{\lambda}\in\arg\min_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathcal{F}_{0}}L(\mathbf{n};\lambda) and let m~s,a:=∑kn~λ,k​(s,a)\tilde{m}_{s,a}:=\sum_{k}\tilde{n}_{\lambda,k}(s,a) be its counts. By exact aggregation and Proposition 9,

Rearranging (77) and using C⁡(𝐧^(t+1))≤κC(\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{(t+1)})\leq\kappa yields

ΔLag(t)\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathrm{Lag}}^{(t)} ≤J~​(𝐧cand(t),𝐧(t))−J~​(𝐧^(t+1),𝐧(t))\displaystyle\leq\tilde{J}(\mathbf{n}_{\mathrm{cand}}^{(t)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})-\tilde{J}(\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{(t+1)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})
≤λ⁡[C⁡(𝐧^(t+1))−C⁡(𝐧cand(t))]+EGreedy(t)\displaystyle\leq\lambda\bigl[C(\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{(t+1)})-C(\mathbf{n}_{\mathrm{cand}}^{(t)})\bigr]+E_{\mathrm{Greedy}}^{(t)}
≤λ⁡[κ−C⁡(𝐧cand(t))]+EGreedy(t).\displaystyle\leq\lambda\bigl[\kappa-C(\mathbf{n}_{\mathrm{cand}}^{(t)})\bigr]+E_{\mathrm{Greedy}}^{(t)}.

If every residual is zero and every factual count is positive, the uniform local bound in Proposition 9 gives the stated bound on EGreedy(t)E_{\mathrm{Greedy}}^{(t)}. ∎

D.5 Per-Iteration Approximation Error

We now combine the majorization and Lagrangian analyses to bound the optimality gap.

Theorem 6 (Per-Iteration Approximation Error).

Let 𝐧∗\mathbf{n}^{*} denote any global minimizer of J⁡(𝐧)J(\mathbf{n}) over ℱ\mathcal{F}, and use any recorded feasible trial and its error certificate from Proposition 10. The solution 𝐧(t+1)\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)} returned by one MM iteration satisfies:

J(𝐧(t+1))−J(𝐧∗)≤∑s∈𝒮d0​(s)​(ℬs​(𝐧∗)−ℬs​(𝐧(t)))2⏟𝒢MM(t):majorization gap+λ(t)​(κ−C⁡(𝐧cand(t)))⏟Lagrangian relaxation gap+EGreedy(t)⏟inner greedy gap.J(\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)})-J(\mathbf{n}^{*})\;\leq\;\underbrace{\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\bigl(\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{*})-\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})\bigr)^{2}}_{\textstyle\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{MM}}^{(t)}\;:\;\text{majorization gap}}\;+\;\underbrace{\lambda^{(t)}\bigl(\kappa-C(\mathbf{n}_{\mathrm{cand}}^{(t)})\bigr)}_{\text{Lagrangian relaxation gap}}\;+\;\underbrace{E_{\mathrm{Greedy}}^{(t)}}_{\text{inner greedy gap}}. (78)

The majorization gap is bounded uniformly by 𝒢MM(t)≤4​βmax2\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{MM}}^{(t)}\leq 4\beta_{\max}^{2}, where βmax\beta_{\max} from Appendix A.4 bounds both annotation biases and default-model biases at zero factual counts. The greedy error certificate includes remaining swap gains when the local search stops at its cap.

Proof.

At fixed tt, the constant difference between J~full\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}} and J~\tilde{J} leaves both the constrained minimizer 𝐧^(t+1)\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{(t+1)} and the value difference ΔLag(t)\Delta_{\mathrm{Lag}}^{(t)} unchanged. Consequently, Lemma 7 and the definition of ΔLag(t)\Delta_{\mathrm{Lag}}^{(t)} in Proposition 10 give

J⁡(𝐧(t+1))\displaystyle J(\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)}) ≤J~full​(𝐧(t+1),𝐧(t))\displaystyle\leq\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}\!\bigl(\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)}\bigr) (majorization)
=J~full​(𝐧^(t+1),𝐧(t))+ΔLag(t)\displaystyle=\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}\!\bigl(\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{(t+1)};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)}\bigr)+\Delta_{\mathrm{Lag}}^{(t)} (definition of ΔLag(t)\Delta_{\mathrm{Lag}}^{(t)})
≤J~full​(𝐧∗,𝐧(t))+ΔLag(t)\displaystyle\leq\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}\!\bigl(\mathbf{n}^{*};\,\mathbf{n}^{(t)}\bigr)+\Delta_{\mathrm{Lag}}^{(t)} (optimality of 𝐧^(t+1)).\displaystyle\text{(optimality of $\hat{\mathbf{n}}^{(t+1)}$)}.

Subtracting J⁡(𝐧∗)J(\mathbf{n}^{*}) and applying the gap formula (70) yields

J⁡(𝐧(t+1))−J⁡(𝐧∗)≤∑s∈𝒮d0​(s)​(ℬs​(𝐧∗)−ℬs​(𝐧(t)))2+ΔLag(t).J(\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)})-J(\mathbf{n}^{*})\leq\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}d_{0}(s)\bigl(\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{*})-\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})\bigr)^{2}+\Delta_{\mathrm{Lag}}^{(t)}.

The upper bound on ΔLag(t)\Delta_{\mathrm{Lag}}^{(t)} from Proposition 10 then gives (78). For N⁡(s,a)>0N(s,a)>0, the bias is a convex combination of zero factual bias and source biases, so |B⁡(s,a)|≤βmax|B(s,a)|\leq\beta_{\max}. For N⁡(s,a)=0N(s,a)=0, the definition of βmax\beta_{\max} also bounds the default bias. Because the target-policy probabilities sum to one, |ℬs|≤βmax|\mathcal{B}_{s}|\leq\beta_{\max}, and hence |ℬs​(𝐧∗)−ℬs​(𝐧(t))|≤2​βmax|\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{*})-\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)})|\leq 2\beta_{\max}. Summing the squared differences with weights d0​(s)d_{0}(s), which also sum to one, gives 𝒢MM(t)≤4​βmax2\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{MM}}^{(t)}\leq 4\beta_{\max}^{2}. ∎

D.6 Convergence Guarantees

Corollary 4 (Finite Descent and Stopping Criteria).

With fixed problem inputs and deterministic tie-breaking, Algorithm 1 has the following properties:

  1. (i)

    Every changed allocation strictly decreases JJ, and there are at most |ℱ|−1|\mathcal{F}|-1 such updates.

  2. (ii)

    If the outer iteration limit is removed and ϵ=0\epsilon=0, the algorithm reaches an unchanged allocation in finitely many iterations. This allocation is a fixed point of the deterministic update rule. A positive tolerance or finite iteration limit may terminate before a fixed point is reached.

  3. (iii)

    If an unchanged allocation 𝐧(∞)\mathbf{n}^{(\infty)} is reached at iteration t⋆t_{\star}, then

    J⁡(𝐧(∞))−J⁡(𝐧∗)\displaystyle J(\mathbf{n}^{(\infty)})-J(\mathbf{n}^{*}) ≤∑sd0​(s)​(ℬs​(𝐧∗)−ℬs​(𝐧(∞)))2\displaystyle\leq\sum_{s}d_{0}(s)\bigl(\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{*})-\mathcal{B}_{s}(\mathbf{n}^{(\infty)})\bigr)^{2} (79)
    +λ(t⋆)​(κ−C⁡(𝐧cand(t⋆)))+EGreedy(t⋆),\displaystyle+\lambda^{(t_{\star})}\bigl(\kappa-C(\mathbf{n}_{\mathrm{cand}}^{(t_{\star})})\bigr)+E_{\mathrm{Greedy}}^{(t_{\star})},

    using any feasible trial recorded at t⋆t_{\star}.

Proof.

The best-candidate variable starts at 𝐧(t)\mathbf{n}^{(t)} and changes only on a strict surrogate improvement. Thus any changed allocation satisfies J~full​(𝐧(t+1),𝐧(t))<J~full​(𝐧(t),𝐧(t))\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n}^{(t+1)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)})<\tilde{J}_{\mathrm{full}}(\mathbf{n}^{(t)};\mathbf{n}^{(t)}), and the majorization chain in Proposition 8 gives strict descent of JJ. No changed allocation can therefore revisit a previous allocation in the finite set ℱ\mathcal{F}, proving (i). After at most |ℱ|−1|\mathcal{F}|-1 changes, an update must leave the allocation unchanged. With fixed inputs, search parameters, and tie-breaking, repeating the update at that allocation returns the same result, proving (ii). The practical stopping conditions can stop after a small strict improvement or at the iteration limit, neither of which implies an unchanged next update. At an unchanged update, 𝐧(t⋆+1)=𝐧(t⋆)=𝐧(∞)\mathbf{n}^{(t_{\star}+1)}=\mathbf{n}^{(t_{\star})}=\mathbf{n}^{(\infty)}, so Theorem 6 gives (79), proving (iii). ∎

D.7 Computational Complexity

Proposition 11 (Total Computational Complexity).

Let S=|𝒮|S=|\mathcal{S}|, A=|𝒜|A=|\mathcal{A}|, K=|𝒦|K=|\mathcal{K}|, Nmax=maxs⁡Ns≥1N_{\max}=\max_{s}N_{s}\geq 1, and let Tswap≥1T_{\mathrm{swap}}\geq 1 cap accepted swaps per local call. Let TMMT_{\mathrm{MM}} be the number of outer iterations and TBisT_{\mathrm{Bis}} an upper bound on all subproblem calls per outer iteration, including the zero-multiplier trial, doubling, and bisection. The total complexity of Algorithm 1 is

𝒪⁡(TMM⋅TBis⋅S⋅A⋅(K2​Nmax​Tswap+Nmax2)).\mathcal{O}\!\Bigl(T_{\mathrm{MM}}\cdot T_{\mathrm{Bis}}\cdot S\cdot A\cdot\bigl(K^{2}\,N_{\max}\,T_{\mathrm{swap}}+N_{\max}^{2}\bigr)\Bigr). (80)

For an iteration with dd multiplier doublings and bracket width W>0W>0 before bisection, the number of subproblem calls is 2+d+max⁡{0,⌈log2⁡(W/ϵλ)⌉}2+d+\max\{0,\lceil\log_{2}(W/\epsilon_{\lambda})\rceil\}. The finite-state bound in Proposition 9 also limits the actual number of accepted swaps, regardless of the chosen cap.

Proof.

For a fixed pair and total count, source search accepts at most TswapT_{\mathrm{swap}} swaps and needs at most one additional scan to certify the final residual. Each scan evaluates K⁡(K−1)K(K-1) swaps in 𝒪⁡(K2)\mathcal{O}(K^{2}) by maintaining the sums ∑knk​Ek\sum_{k}n_{k}E_{k}, ∑knk​Dk\sum_{k}n_{k}D_{k}, and ∑kck​nk\sum_{k}c_{k}n_{k}; each accepted swap updates these sums in constant time. Initialization and storing the source vector cost 𝒪⁡(K)\mathcal{O}(K), so the full fixed-count cost is 𝒪⁡(K2​Tswap)\mathcal{O}(K^{2}T_{\mathrm{swap}}) for Tswap≥1T_{\mathrm{swap}}\geq 1. There are at most Nmax+1N_{\max}+1 counts per pair, giving 𝒪⁡(A​Nmax​K2​Tswap)\mathcal{O}(AN_{\max}K^{2}T_{\mathrm{swap}}) per context when Nmax≥1N_{\max}\geq 1. The action-indexed DP has A⁡(Ns+1)A(N_{s}+1) entries, each scanning at most Ns+1N_{s}+1 feasible counts, so aggregation costs 𝒪⁡(A​Nmax2)\mathcal{O}(AN_{\max}^{2}) per context. Backtracking costs 𝒪⁡(A​K)\mathcal{O}(AK), and scanning the residual tables costs 𝒪⁡(A​Nmax)\mathcal{O}(AN_{\max}), both within the preceding bounds. Candidate objective comparisons cost 𝒪⁡(S​A​K)\mathcal{O}(SAK) per trial and are also dominated by the subproblem cost. Summing over contexts, all multiplier trials, and outer iterations proves (80). There are two initial trials, one at zero and one at λ0\lambda_{0}, followed by dd doubling trials. Each bisection trial halves the interval width, giving the stated remaining trial count. ∎

Appendix E Experimental Details and Additional Results

Code and reproduction instructions are available at

https://github.com/Lygist/Budgeted-Multi-Source-Counterfactual-Annotation-for-Off-Policy-Evaluation.

The accompanying README provides detailed instructions on data preparation, configuration, and the execution pipeline.

Computational resources.

Local preprocessing, allocation, and OPE calculations used only the central processing unit (CPU) of a MacBook with an Apple M3 Pro chip; the codebase is also compatible with the standard Google Colab CPU environment. LLM annotations were obtained through hosted application programming interfaces (APIs) from Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic. Table 7 reports full-instance solver runtimes, with a one-hour limit for each Gurobi run. Theoretical runtime bounds are given in Proposition 3 and Appendix D.7.

E.1 Synthetic Clinical Bandit

E.1.1 Environment and source profiles

We use 100100 contexts and 55 actions. For each context, πb(⋅∣s)∼Dirichlet(0.2𝟏)\pi_{b}(\cdot\mid s)\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(0.2\mathbf{1}). The target policy retains a behavior-selected action with probability 0.90.9 and otherwise replaces it by a uniformly sampled alternative. The context distribution is sampled from a symmetric Dirichlet distribution.

Pairwise reward means are independently drawn from

0.2​Normal⁡(−2,32)+0.8​SkewNormal⁡(ξ=5,ω=6,α=−2),0.2\,\operatorname{Normal}(-2,3^{2})+0.8\,\operatorname{SkewNormal}(\xi=5,\omega=6,\alpha=-2),

and reward variances from Uniform⁡(20,50)\operatorname{Uniform}(20,50). The fitting dataset contains M=1,000M=1{,}000 records. Source kk has mean μr​(s,a)+εk\mu_{r}(s,a)+\varepsilon_{k}, variance σr2​(s,a)+Δk\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a)+\Delta_{k}, and cost ckc_{k}. The allocation budget is κ=10,000\kappa=10{,}000.

E.1.2 Source Subset Comparison Under Consistent Optimization

To isolate the effect of source availability from allocation strategy, we evaluate all nonempty subsets 𝒦sub⊆{1,2,3,4}\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{sub}}\subseteq\{1,2,3,4\} with MM, including the single-source subsets evaluated under random allocation in Figure 2. Figure 3 shows the resulting scaled MSE values. Under consistent optimization, the qualitative conclusions of §7 are unchanged.

E.1.3 Convergence Trace on the Synthetic Bandit

Figure 4 reports the convergence trace of the MM algorithm on the synthetic clinical bandit, replayed across the source subsets that achieve successively lower scaled MSE values: {1,3}\{1,3\}, {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\}, and finally {1,2,3,4}\{1,2,3,4\}. Scaled MSE drops sharply within the first MM iteration of each subset and stabilizes within roughly 55–66 iterations, consistent with the monotone-descent property in Proposition 8. The annotation-count tuples annotated on the trajectory show that the optimizer concentrates the budget on the lowest-bias source (Source 1) at first and progressively allocates a small share to higher-variance, lower-cost sources as additional sources become available.

E.2 ASSISTments Semi-Synthetic Environment

E.2.1 Dataset, Context Space, and Action Space

The ASSISTments 2012–13 School Data with Affect [5] contains 6,123,2706{,}123{,}270 student–problem interactions from the ASSISTments online middle-school mathematics tutoring platform. Each row records: (i) student/problem identifiers, (ii) first-response latency ms_first_response, (iii) correctness of first attempt, hint count, and attempt count, (iv) problem metadata (problem_type, original indicator), and (v) four affect-detector confidences (frustration, confusion, concentration, boredom). We remove interactions with ms_first_response outside [1,000, 600,000][1{,}000,\;600{,}000] ms (<1<1 s likely auto-fill, >10>10 min likely idle), retaining 6,117,2796{,}117{,}279 rows (99.9%99.9\%), then sort by (user_id, start_time) so that past statistics use only strictly prior interactions.

Context Space (|𝒮|=100|\mathcal{S}|=100)

Each interaction is embedded as a 6-dimensional vector

ϕcontext=[PastCorrect,PastHints,Frust,Conf,Conc,Bore],\phi_{\mathrm{context}}=\bigl[\mathrm{PastCorrect},\;\mathrm{PastHints},\;\mathrm{Frust},\;\mathrm{Conf},\;\mathrm{Conc},\;\mathrm{Bore}\bigr],

where PastCorrect\mathrm{PastCorrect} and PastHints\mathrm{PastHints} are expanding-mean correct rate and hint count over the student’s strictly prior problems (initialized to 0.50.5 and 00). Features are standardized; K-means with k=100k{=}100, ninit=10n_{\mathrm{init}}{=}10 produces 100100 clusters. Centroids in the original scale are passed to the LLM as the context descriptor.

Action Space (|𝒜|=10|\mathcal{A}|=10)

We cross problem_type (6 values) with original (2 values), then retain the 1010 combinations with at least 100100 observed interactions. Table 5 lists the resulting actions and their empirical statistics used both in the reward function and in the LLM prompt.

E.2.2 Reward Function

Following the feature-prediction spirit of APRIL [4], we decompose the reward into a data-driven base and an LLM-predictable multiplier. With Rmax=30R_{\max}=30:

R⁡(s,a,t)=Rmax⋅PIRT​(s,a)⏟data-driven⋅TimeEff⁡(t,t~a)⏟LLM-predictable.R(s,a,t)\;=\;R_{\max}\cdot\underbrace{P_{\mathrm{IRT}}(s,a)}_{\text{data-driven}}\cdot\underbrace{\mathrm{TimeEff}(t,\tilde{t}_{a})}_{\text{LLM-predictable}}. (81)
IRT component.

For context ss with centroid correct rate psp_{s} and action aa with overall correct rate qaq_{a}, set θs=logit⁡(ps)\theta_{s}=\mathrm{logit}(p_{s}), ba=logit⁡(1−qa)b_{a}=\mathrm{logit}(1-q_{a}), and PIRT​(s,a)=σ⁡(θs−ba)P_{\mathrm{IRT}}(s,a)=\sigma(\theta_{s}-b_{a}), with ps,qap_{s},q_{a} clipped to [0.02,0.98][0.02,0.98]. This is a Rasch (1-PL) model depending only on observed data. Across the 100×10100\times 10 grid, PIRTP_{\mathrm{IRT}} has range [0.03,0.98][0.03,0.98], mean 0.680.68, std 0.220.22—providing the primary reward variation.

Time-efficiency component.

Let t~a\tilde{t}_{a} be action aa’s median response time in seconds. Define

TimeEff⁡(t,t~a)=max⁡{0.3, 1−α⋅|log10⁡(t/t~a)|},α=0.4.\mathrm{TimeEff}(t,\tilde{t}_{a})\;=\;\max\!\left\{0.3,\;1-\alpha\cdot\bigl|\log_{10}(t/\tilde{t}_{a})\bigr|\right\},\quad\alpha=0.4.

This symmetric clamped-linear function is 1.01.0 at t=t~at=\tilde{t}_{a}, decays linearly in log-space, and floors at 0.30.3 for extreme mispredictions. This constructed discount encodes a preference for response times near the action-specific median, penalizing both unusually short and unusually long responses.

Ground-truth reward.

For each observed (s,a)(s,a) pair, the reference μr​(s,a)\mu_{r}(s,a) is computed by plugging the empirical median t~s,a\tilde{t}_{s,a} into Eq. (81). For the 54/100054/1000 pairs with fewer than 2020 observations, we fit a random forest on context centroids ++ action one-hot features to predict log10⁡t~s,a\log_{10}\tilde{t}_{s,a} (55-fold CV R2=0.89R^{2}=0.89) and fill the gap. The final μr\mu_{r} grid has range [0.43,28.7][0.43,28.7], mean 20.0820.08, std 10.7710.77.

E.2.3 LLM Prompt Design

Each prompt is a batch of 1010 (s,a)(s,a) pairs sharing a common task description, action-reference table, and domain-knowledge preamble, followed by pair-specific student profiles and 88 bootstrap-sampled historical response times per pair. All per-pair information (ability-level label, centroid features, action statistics, historical samples) is precomputed once from the dataframe before any API call, keeping per-batch overhead below 11 ms and the mean prompt length at ∼3,500\sim\!3{,}500 characters. Figure 6 shows the template; curly-braced fields are populated from precomputed lookups.

E.2.4 LLM Annotation Allocation by MM

We evaluate four LLM annotation sources: Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-o3-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5. For each of the 100×10100\times 10 context-action pairs, each model produces 2020 first-response-time predictions at temperature 0.80.8, yielding 20,00020{,}000 predictions per model. We estimate each source’s bias as ε^k​(s,a)=r¯k​(s,a)−μr​(s,a)\hat{\varepsilon}_{k}(s,a)=\bar{r}_{k}(s,a)-\mu_{r}(s,a), where r¯k​(s,a)\bar{r}_{k}(s,a) is the mean of the 2020 predicted rewards and μr​(s,a)\mu_{r}(s,a) is the reference reward from the simulator. We estimate prediction variability by σ^k​(s,a)\hat{\sigma}_{k}(s,a), the standard deviation of the 2020 predicted rewards. Table 6 summarizes these estimates and the API costs. GPT-4o-mini has the lowest mean absolute bias and cost, while GPT-o3-mini costs about 78×78\times more without improving the reported quality summaries, consistent with the feature-prediction findings of APRIL [4].

We generate 6,0006{,}000 logged samples from the ASSISTments simulator, with pair-specific reward variances σr2​(s,a)∼Uniform⁡(30,60)\sigma_{r}^{2}(s,a)\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(30,60). Based on the source diagnostics in Table 6, we run the MM-based allocation algorithm with the three lower-cost sources, excluding GPT-o3-mini, under budget κ=$0.50\kappa=\$0.50. The algorithm decides to purchase 6,0006{,}000 annotations and reduces the variance objective from J⁡(𝟎)=88.61J(\mathbf{0})=88.61 to 79.0679.06, a 10.77%10.77\% reduction.

Mirroring the synthetic experiment, we evaluate every non-empty LLM source subset (excluding the high-cost GPT-o3-mini, which Table 6 shows offers no quality advantage) under two protocols for the single source baseline: a uniformly random allocation and the proposed MM algorithm.

Figure 7 reports the random-allocation baseline. Single-source subsets yield variance objectives in the range 80.7980.79–83.7283.72, while every multi-source subset drops below 8080.

Figure 8 repeats the comparison under consistent MM optimization. The single-source bars improve to 79.3279.32–80.8280.82, narrowing the gap to multi-source results. The three-source configuration {Gemini,Claude,GPT-4o-mini}\{\text{Gemini},\text{Claude},\text{GPT-4o-mini}\} remains the global optimum at J=79.06J=79.06, a 10.77%10.77\% reduction over J⁡(𝟎)=88.61J(\mathbf{0})=88.61.

To illustrate the dynamics of the MM algorithm under realistic LLM annotation profiles, Figure 9 shows the convergence trace on ASSISTments. The objective decreases monotonically from 88.6188.61 to 79.0679.06.

E.3 Exact-Solver Benchmarks and Runtime

To complement the certified small-instance optima in Table 4, we warm-started Gurobi on the full Synthetic and ASSISTments instances with the best heuristic solution and imposed a one-hour time limit. The runs did not certify global optimality within that limit, so we compare the methods against the valid lower bounds available at termination. Let LL be the scaled-MSE lower bound available at termination and zA=𝒱⁡(𝐧A)z_{A}=\mathcal{V}(\mathbf{n}_{A}) the scaled MSE returned by method AA. The table reports 100​(zA−L)/zA100(z_{A}-L)/z_{A}. The heuristic runtimes exclude the Gurobi computation used to obtain LL.

Table 4 shows greedy-initialized MM has a 0.05%0.05\% mean gap and a 0.26%0.26\% maximum gap to the certified optima on the small instances. On the full instances, Table 7 shows that it reaches within 0.2807%0.2807\% and 0.0050%0.0050\% of the Gurobi lower bounds in 5.35.3 and 522522 seconds, respectively. These comparisons show small empirical gaps to the available exact and lower-bound benchmarks.

E.4 End-to-End Evaluation with Finite Pilots

The solver benchmarks assess optimization quality for fixed profiles; we next evaluate final OPE performance when allocations are selected using finite-pilot estimates. For each of 3030 pilot replications, factual moments are estimated from 2020 pilot rewards per pair and annotation moments from 2020 pilot draws per source–pair. The pilot is separate from subsequent fitting rewards, acquired annotation realizations, and OPE outcomes. Fitting-data context–action counts determine the capacities.

Each allocator receives the same pilot estimates and constraints. For the optimized single-source baseline, we optimize each source separately and use the pilot objective to select the predicted best source. Thus, this baseline does not select its source using final OPE outcomes.

After fixing an allocation, we generated 5050 independent reward and annotation realizations from the distributions used in each environment and evaluated DM+-IS on independent OPE datasets (N=1,000N=1{,}000 for Synthetic and N=6,000N=6{,}000 for ASSISTments). In ASSISTments, the annotation realizations are drawn from empirical source models fitted to the observed LLM predictions. Within each pilot replication, empirical MSE is the average squared deviation of the 5050 final value estimates from the environment’s true policy value. Table 8 reports the mean across pilot replications of the relative MSE reduction versus the corresponding no-annotation baseline.

Table 8 shows greedy-initialized MM reduces empirical MSE by 19.13%19.13\% on Synthetic and 8.47%8.47\% on ASSISTments relative to no annotation. Thus, the allocation gains persist in these experiments after finite-sample profile estimation and evaluation of the final OPE estimator.

E.5 Within-pair bootstrap

As a complementary check, we assess sensitivity to resampling the LLM outputs used to estimate source profiles. For each of 3030 bootstrap replications, we resample the 2020 observed predictions within each source–pair, re-estimate its moments, and rerun MM. We evaluate the resulting allocation using reference profiles estimated from all 2020 original predictions per source–pair.

The average reference-profile MSE reduction is 10.765%10.765\%, compared with 10.774%10.774\% using the original profiles. The standard deviation is 0.00380.0038 percentage points, and the mean difference is 0.0090.009 percentage points. This measures conditional sensitivity to resampling the observed outputs. Because evaluation uses the same empirical source reference, it is not held-out validation of the population LLM distribution and does not measure uncertainty in the simulator’s factual reward reference.

Appendix F Broader Impacts and Asset Use

F.1 Broader Impacts

Budgeted counterfactual annotation can improve the efficiency of policy evaluation before deployment. In healthcare and education, unreliable annotations or violations of the evaluation assumptions may nevertheless yield inaccurate policy comparisons with consequences for treatment or instruction. Application-specific validation, including assessment of subgroup outcomes, is therefore important before deployment.

F.2 Existing Data and Model Services

The ASSISTments 2012–13 School Data with Affect [5, 6] are provided by Neil T. Heffernan and the ASSISTments team at Worcester Polytechnic Institute through the official dataset release. The ASSISTments data-use conditions require users to report and delete any inadvertently discovered personally identifiable information and prohibit using that information. Our experiments use existing records, with no participant recruitment, crowdsourcing, or interventions.

The annotation sources are Google’s Gemini-2.5-Flash, OpenAI’s GPT-4o-mini, and Anthropic’s Claude-Haiku-4.5. Hosted access is subject to the Google APIs Terms of Service and Gemini API Additional Terms of Service, the OpenAI Services Agreement, and the Anthropic Commercial Terms of Service, respectively.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The claims in the abstract and introduction match the theoretical results proved in Appendices A–D and the experimental results in Section 7.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

    Limitations

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: The Conclusion discusses the contextual-bandit scope, reliance on known or estimated source profiles, and semi-synthetic ASSISTments environment. Sensitivity to estimated profiles is analyzed in Appendix A.4 and evaluated in Section 7.3.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [Yes]

  14. Justification: Assumptions accompany the theoretical statements, and their derivations and proofs are provided in Appendices A–D.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: Section 7 and Appendix E describe the environments, reward functions, large language model (LLM) prompts, and evaluation protocols; code and reproduction instructions are available at the GitHub repository link in Appendix E.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general, releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  21. 5.

    Open access to data and code

  22. Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  23. Answer: [Yes]

  24. Justification: We provide a GitHub repository containing all code, public data sources, data preprocessing scripts, and a detailed README to reproduce the experiments. See details in Appendix E.

  25. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

    • •

      Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

    • •

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  26. 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  28. Answer: [Yes]

  29. Justification: Section 7 and Appendix E describe the synthetic and semi-synthetic environments, preprocessing, source-profile estimation, and separation of pilot, fitting, and evaluation samples.

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: We report the mean and standard deviation across 100 independent environment initializations(e.g., shaded bands in Figure 1). We also provide bootstraps experiment to test the robustness of the algorithm in Section 7.3.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: Appendix E identifies the local hardware and hosted LLM services, and Table 7 reports full-instance solver runtimes. Memory, runtimes for the remaining experiments, and total project compute are not reported.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: The research conforms to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: Appendix F.1 discusses the benefit of more efficient policy evaluation, potential consequences of inaccurate policy comparisons, and the need for application-specific validation.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: The contribution is an allocation method using existing data and hosted LLMs; we do not release a pretrained generative model or a newly collected student dataset.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  56. 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  58. Answer: [Yes]

  59. Justification: Appendix F.2 identifies the ASSISTments release and creators, links its data-use conditions, and identifies the LLM providers and applicable service terms.

  60. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

    • •

      The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.

    • •

      The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.

    • •

      The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.

    • •

      For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  61. 13.

    New assets

  62. Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?

  63. Answer: [Yes]

  64. Justification: The code and detailed instructions are in our repository at [repository URL].

  65. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.

    • •

      Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.

    • •

      The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.

    • •

      At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.

  66. 14.

    Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects

  67. Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?

  68. Answer: [N/A]

  69. Justification: We use synthetic data and secondary analysis of existing ASSISTments records, with no participant recruitment, crowdsourcing, or interventions (Appendix F.2).

  70. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

    • •

      According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.

  71. 15.

    Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

  72. Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?

  73. Answer: [N/A]

  74. Justification: The experiments use synthetic data and secondary analysis of the public ASSISTments release, with no new participant recruitment or interventions (Appendix F.2).

  75. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.

    • •

      We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.

    • •

      For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review.

  78. Answer: [Yes]
